Canada Develops Article 6 Framework to Expand International Carbon Markets
- Canada is exploring a framework for trading internationally transferred mitigation outcomes (ITMOs) under Article 6 of the Paris Agreement.
- The framework could channel investment into carbon removal, nature-based solutions and other high-integrity mitigation projects in Canada and overseas.
- Federal officials see international carbon markets as a route to scale Canadian climate technologies, attract private capital and strengthen clean-economy exports.
The federal government is developing a policy framework that could open Canadian companies to a larger international market for carbon credits under the Paris Agreement.
The Honourable Julie Dabrusin, Minister of the Environment, Climate Change and Nature, announced that Canada is exploring how to trade internationally transferred mitigation outcomes, known as ITMOs.
The approach could allow Canadian businesses to participate more extensively in international carbon markets. Ottawa expects this could catalyze investment in climate mitigation, including carbon removal technologies and nature-based solutions.
For Canada, the policy has both climate and industrial implications. The country has extensive geological storage potential, clean power resources and established industrial expertise. Federal policymakers are seeking ways to turn those advantages into investment and export opportunities as more economies pursue decarbonization.
Article 6 opens another route for climate finance
Article 6 of the Paris Agreement allows countries to cooperate in meeting their national climate targets. This can include transferring verified emissions reductions or removals between countries through ITMOs.
Such transactions could direct capital toward projects that generate high-integrity mitigation outcomes in Canada and abroad. They could also create new markets for Canadian carbon management technologies and technical expertise.
“The trading of ITMOs under the Paris Agreement can unlock greater global climate action by making it easier to transfer emission reductions and removals between countries. This is about turning our natural advantages and homegrown climate innovation into investment, good jobs, and new export opportunities. A clear framework for international carbon credit transfers can help Canadian companies scale, attract capital, and bring more innovative technologies to market, strengthening our position as a leader in the global clean economy.” – The Honourable Julie Dabrusin, Minister of the Environment, Climate Change and Nature
The economic opportunity could be substantial. Carbon Removal Canada estimates that a scaled carbon dioxide removal industry could contribute billions of dollars to Canadian GDP by 2050 and support hundreds of thousands of jobs.
The proposed ITMO framework also follows Canada’s Spring Economic Update, which committed more than $13 billion to international climate finance. The government said this places Canada among the first countries to announce international climate finance pledges extending beyond 2026.
RELATED ARTICLE: Canada Backs $70B Clean Power Buildout
Integrity rules will shape the market
For investors and companies, the credibility of any future Canadian ITMO market will depend heavily on accounting and environmental integrity.
Carbon credits transferred as ITMOs must comply with Article 6 requirements. Reductions or removals must be additional to what would otherwise have occurred. Countries must also prevent the same mitigation outcome from being counted toward both the exporting and importing country’s climate targets.
Participating governments therefore need institutional systems capable of tracking and accounting for greenhouse gas reductions and removals.
Canada said any future ITMO trading would follow Article 6 rules and guidance. The government intends to ensure traded reductions and removals are real, additional, verified and permanent.
Clear accounting standards will also be important for private capital. Greater certainty around authorization, ownership and recognition of credits could reduce risks for investors financing long-term carbon removal projects.
Canada weighs its role in a growing carbon market
Ottawa will consult provinces and territories, Indigenous organizations and other partners as it considers how an ITMO system could operate domestically.
The government is also examining other policies compatible with a net-zero economy, including the potential use of international and domestic offset credits.
For executives and investors, the framework could eventually connect Canadian climate projects with a broader pool of international buyers and capital. Carbon removal developers may be among the most closely affected, particularly if clear rules improve the commercial case for scaling technologies.
The wider significance reaches beyond Canada. As countries put Article 6 into practice, governance and accounting standards will determine whether international carbon markets can attract capital while maintaining environmental credibility. Canada’s proposed framework adds another major economy to that evolving system.

articles.full_text:
GRI to Launch New Sustainability Reporting Standard for Food and Beverage Companies
- GRI is developing its first dedicated Sector Standard for food and beverage companies, covering impacts across operations and global value chains.
- The standard will pilot a streamlined development process designed to deliver sector-specific reporting guidance faster while retaining multistakeholder review.
- GRI research found 43% of listed food and beverage companies report using GRI, representing 70% of the sector’s global market capitalization.
The Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) is developing a new sustainability reporting standard for the global food and beverage industry, targeting a sector exposed to climate, biodiversity, labor and public health risks across complex supply chains.
The Food and Beverages Sector Standard will provide industry-specific guidance on the sustainability impacts companies are most likely to consider material. It will cover companies’ own operations as well as value chains connected to agriculture, aquaculture and fishing.
GRI has selected food and beverages as the first sector to test a faster model for developing its Sector Standards. The approach aims to reduce development timelines while maintaining GRI’s established multistakeholder due process.
Reporting focus moves deeper into value chains
Food and beverage companies operate across supply chains that connect farms, fisheries and processing facilities with manufacturers, retailers and consumers. That reach creates significant exposure to environmental and social issues.
The new standard will identify sustainability topics likely to be material for companies in the sector. It will also summarize the industry’s most significant impacts and direct companies toward relevant existing GRI Topic Standards.
For companies, the framework could provide greater clarity over which impacts warrant disclosure. For investors and other stakeholders, more consistent reporting could improve comparisons across businesses operating in different markets and supply chains.
“The food and beverage sector touches almost every part of society, while its value chains are closely connected with some of the most pressing sustainability challenges we face. From climate change and biodiversity loss to working conditions and public health, companies need to understand and transparently report their impacts. This new GRI Sector Standard will provide focused guidance on the issues that matter most, helping companies deliver more consistent reporting, and the information needed for decision making that improves sustainability performance and business resilience. As the first pilot for a more streamlined approach, we need input from the sector and its stakeholders. I encourage those with relevant expertise to get involved and help us ensure the Standard is practical, credible, and reflects the realities of this global industry.” Peter Dawkins, GRI Standards Senior Manager
RELATED ARICLE: Global Reporting Initiative (GRI) Appoints Robin Hodess as New CEO
GRI seeks global experts for peer review
GRI is seeking up to 20 experts worldwide to join a multistakeholder Peer Review Group. Applications are open until October 23, 2026.
Their input will help test whether the streamlined development model can accelerate standard-setting without weakening credibility or industry relevance.
The process has broader implications beyond food and beverages. Demand for sustainability information continues to expand, while companies face growing pressure to navigate different disclosure frameworks and stakeholder expectations.
A faster route to sector-specific guidance could help GRI respond more quickly to those demands. It may also make the organization’s existing reporting architecture easier to apply in industries where sustainability impacts vary substantially by sector.
Food companies already have high GRI adoption
The initiative builds on significant existing use of GRI reporting within the industry.
GRI’s June 2026 State of Sustainability Reporting research examined almost 15,000 listed companies worldwide. It found that 43% of food and beverage companies report using GRI. Those companies account for 70% of the sector’s global market capitalization.
The new standard will apply to organizations involved in food and drink processing and manufacturing, including tobacco products.
GRI already has Sector Standards covering oil and gas, coal, mining, agriculture, aquaculture and fishing. The food and beverage standard will be the first created through the streamlined development model.
What companies and investors should watch
GRI Sector Standards sit within a modular reporting framework. Companies begin with the Universal Standards, use applicable Sector Standards to identify material topics, and then report through the relevant Topic Standards.
For food and beverage executives, the forthcoming standard could influence how businesses organize impact assessments, sustainability data and value-chain disclosures. Companies using GRI may need to examine whether existing reporting captures the sector-specific issues identified in the final standard.
Investors could also gain more comparable information on risks that extend beyond direct operations, particularly those connected with agricultural sourcing, biodiversity, labor conditions and climate exposure.
The pilot therefore carries significance beyond one industry. Its success could determine whether GRI can expand sector-specific guidance more quickly while preserving the stakeholder scrutiny that underpins its standards globally.

articles.summary: The Ultimate Guide to Understanding Carbon Credits  CarbonCredits.com
articles.full_text:
For many investors, carbon offsets are a way to minimize their own carbon footprint and live an environmentally friendly lifestyle. The size of the market and the growing demand for carbon offsets indicate that there’s serious potential for companies that produce carbon credits to see large-scale growth over the next decades.
15. Do I Need Carbon Offsets or Carbon Credits?
Now that you know their differences and what they have in common, here’s how carbon credits and carbon offsets work in the grand, global scheme of emissions reduction.
The government is putting heavy caps on greenhouse gas emissions, meaning that companies will have to reconfigure their operations to reduce emissions as much as possible. Those that cannot be eliminated will have to be accounted for through the purchase of carbon credits.
Ambitious organizations, corporations, and people can purchase carbon offsets to reach net zero or even nullify all previous historical emissions.
So which do you need?
If you’re a corporation, the answer might just be “both” — but it all depends on your business goals, as well as the local regulations where your company operates. If you’re a consumer, carbon credits are likely unavailable to you, but you can still do your part by purchasing carbon offsets.
Returning to the illustration from earlier, our vital, global goal is to both stop dumping chemicals into the metaphorical water supply and to purify the existing water supply over time. In other words, we need to both drastically reduce CO2 emissions and work to remove the CO2 currently in the atmosphere if we want to materially reduce pollution.
16. Why Should I Buy Carbon Credits?
If you’re a corporation, there are plenty of compelling reasons as to why you should be seriously considering investing in carbon credits and offsets.
If you’re an individual looking to buy carbon credits, you’re likely interested in one of two reasons:
The first reason is that you’re environmentally conscious and looking to do your part in combating climate change by offsetting your own greenhouse gas emissions, or those of your family.
If that’s the case, then rest assured – carbon offsets from a reputable vendor such as Native Energy are the perfect way for you to negate your own carbon footprint.
The second reason you’re interested in buying carbon credits is that you think it represents an investment opportunity. The global carbon market grew 20% last year, and that strong growth is expected to continue as climate change becomes an increasingly relevant concern to the world at large.
If you fall into the latter category, then head over to our carbon investor center, where we showcase some of the best investment opportunities in the carbon sector right now.
17. What is Blue Carbon?
Blue Carbon are special carbon credit derived from sites known as blue carbon ecosystems. These ecosystems primarily feature marine forests, such as tidal marshes, mangrove forests, and seagrass beds.
Yes, forests can grow in the ocean! Examples include the mangrove forests in sea bays, such as Magdalena Bay in Baja California Sur, Mexico.
Mangroves are trees (about 70 percent underwater, 30 percent above water) that have evolved to be able to survive in flooded coastal environments where seawater meets freshwater, and the resulting lack of oxygen makes life impossible for other plants.
- Key Fact: Mangroves cover just 0.1% of Earth’s surface
Mangrove trees create shelter and food for numerous species such as sharks, whales, and sea turtles. And thanks to their other second-order effects, such as the positive impacts on corals, algae, and marine biodiversity that have been so negatively impacted by activities such as over-fishing and farming, mangroves are considered to be extremely valuable marine ecosystems.
Over the past decade, scientists have discovered that blue carbon ecosystems like these mangrove forests are among the most intensive carbon sinks in the world.
Accordingly, a blue carbon offset project will have its carbon offsets traded at a premium.
18. Second-order Effects of Blue Carbon Credits
Other positive second-order effects of mangrove forests include:
- Their importance as a pollution filter,
- Reducing coastal wave energy, and
- Reducing the impacts of coastal storms and extreme events.
Blue carbon systems also trap sediment, which supports root systems for more plants.
This accumulation of sediment over time can enable coastal habitats to keep pace with rising sea levels.
In addition, because the carbon is sequestered and stored below water in aquatic forests and wetlands, it’s stored for more than ten times longer than in tropical forests.
- The significant positive second-order effects attributed to each blue carbon credit are why many believe they will trade at a premium to other carbon credits.
Blue Carbon and the Food Footprint
There is a land-use carbon footprint of 1,440 kg CO2e for every kilogram of beef and 1,603 kg CO2e for every kilogram of shrimp produced on lands formerly occupied by mangroves. A typical steak and shrimp cocktail dinner would potentially burden the atmosphere with 816 kg CO2e if the ingredients were to come from such sources.
It’s estimated that over 1 billion tons of CO2 are released annually from degrading coastal ecosystems.
There are around 14 million hectares of mangrove aquaforests on Earth today. Many are under attack by the deforestation practices caused by intense shrimp farming
Are the shrimp you eat part of the problem? Soon, these shrimps will be labeled, and consumers will know and be required to cover the offset costs for the environmental damage.
To put things into perspective, 14 million acres of wetlands would absorb as much carbon out of the atmosphere as if all of California and New York State were covered in tropical rainforests.
Think of blue carbon as the “high-grade” gold mine at the surface.
Oceanic Blue Carbon
In addition to the coastal blue carbon mentioned above, oceanic blue carbon is stored deep in the ocean within phytoplankton and other open ocean biota.

There are many factors that influence carbon capture by blue carbon ecosystems. These include:
- Location
- Depth of water
- Plant species
- Supply of nutrients
Improving blue carbon ecosystems can significantly improve the livelihoods and cultural practices of local and traditional communities. In addition, restoring blue carbon regions provides enormous biodiversity benefits to both marine and terrestrial species.

articles.title: What will Europe’s latest greenwashing regime mean for investors? - Responsible Investor
articles.summary: What will Europe’s latest greenwashing regime mean for investors?  Responsible Investor
articles.full_text:
By the end of this week, one of the world’s most ambitious anti-greenwashing regimes will be fully applicable across Europe.
The Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition (ECGT) Directive, nicknamed EmpCo, will update the EU’s existing Unfair Commercial Practices Directive (UCPD) with more explicit rules around sustainability claims.
“It will go a lot further than almost any other regulation or legislation in the world,” says Renske Mackor, director of regulatory and sustainability risk at PwC Netherlands. “Any statement that a business makes in the context of a commercial activity towards consumers falls within the scope.”
EmpCo places major restrictions on how firms can communicate about their goods, services and brands, including by banning generic, vague or exaggerated claims. “Saying your company is sustainable, for example, is prohibited unless you can prove it with a recognised external certification or label,” says Mackor.
More specific claims have to be substantiated with clear evidence, and forward-looking claims must be expressed as serious, timebound targets.
“You won’t be able to just say you’ll be net zero by 2050 anymore – you’ll have to have an implementation plan that’s reviewed and verified by a third party on an ongoing basis,” says Mackor. “And carbon offsetting claims will only be permitted if they relate to offsets undertaken within the value chain of that particular product. Anything else is prohibited.”
Investor implications
While the ECGT Directive is usually talked about in the context of physical goods and services, it also covers financial ones – including all investment funds and pension products made directly available to European retail investors, even if the primary audience is professional investors.
“Vague green claims mislead people, whether they’re buying a washing machine or a fund,” says Anyve Arakelijan, a senior regulatory policy adviser at the European Fund and Asset Management Association (EFAMA).
However, she says, some of EmpCo’s tests were designed with physical items in mind, and are not well-suited to investment products – such as the requirement for words like “green” or “sustainable” to be used only when accompanied by proof of excellent environmental performance.
“For a physical product, that makes sense – you can measure its footprint, and you can certify it,” says Arakelijan. “A fund is different. What makes a fund sustainable is how it invests – what it holds, what it excludes, what methodology it uses, and what it discloses to investors.”
As she notes, Europe’s investment industry already has two sets of greenwashing rules – the Sustainable Finance Disclosure Regulation (SFDR) and guidance from the European Securities and Markets Authority (ESMA) on using terms like ESG or sustainable in fund names.
Regulation overlap
A key question for investors will be how EmpCo fits with the EU’s other greenwashing rules. Every part of the Unfair Commercial Practices Directive can be overridden if another, more appropriate consumer protection regime already exists.
“The discussion now is whether SFDR fulfills that definition,” says Heike Schmitz, a senior lawyer specialising in sustainable finance at Herbert Smith Freehills.
And, according to the European Commission, it does.
“For sustainability-related disclosures that it specifically regulates, [SFDR] takes precedence over more general consumer-law rules,” said a spokesperson. “The UCPD does not impose parallel or conflicting requirements on elements that are specifically regulated by the SFDR.”
The Commission has proposed a clarification in the next iteration of SFDR to make it explicit that the legislation functions as a consumer protection regime, and therefore supersedes EmpCo’s rules.
“Absurdly, this is taken as an argument by some in the market to say that, if the Commission takes the step to clarify it, it is fair to assume the current SFDR is not explicitly seen as a specialised consumer protection law,” says Schmitz. “And that’s the version that’s in place for the time being.”
That’s the position taken by EFAMA, in lieu of official guidance.
“Under the Commission’s SFDR 2.0 proposal, the idea is that if you follow SFDR properly, you also meet the consumer protection requirements. But that is still being negotiated and isn’t expected to apply before 2028,” says Arakelijan.
“So for about two years, the same fund communication may be checked twice, by financial supervisors and by consumer authorities or civil courts, using different criteria.”
ESMA’s guidelines will create another complication, she adds.
For instance, they permit a fund to be called “sustainable” if at least 80 percent of its investments are used to meet its environmental or social characteristics or sustainability objectives, and it applies strict exclusions.
“The risk is that a court could still treat the term ‘sustainable’ as a generic environmental claim under EmpCo, and ban it unless the fund can show ‘recognised excellent environmental performance’ – a test built for physical products,” says Arakelijan. “So a fund that follows its financial rules could still be challenged in court.”
The Commission says EmpCo will “operate as a horizontal and complementary safety net for aspects that are not specifically governed by sector-specific legislation, including the overall presentation of environmental claims to consumers”.
This means entity-level descriptions like “responsible investor”, or common assurances such as “sustainability is in our DNA”, must be clearly evidenced.
Climate targets or net-zero pledges made available to consumers to help sell products or services will now have to be communicated as quantitative targets with deadlines, backed by a verified transition plan and updated at regular intervals.
“You can’t claim your whole organisation is going green unless it really is the whole organisation,” says Marcus Navin-Jones, senior counsel and environmental specialist at law firm Crowell & Moring.
But there is confusion about whether, under the Commission’s definition, EmpCo still might be applied to certain product-level claims as well.
“It’s unclear what would happen if you use information you’ve disclosed in compliance with SFDR within your marketing materials, too,” says Schmitz.
“Is a statement that’s acceptable in the context of SFDR now subject to a different set of rules once it becomes marketing? If you say your emissions have reduced by X percent over a period as part of your SFDR reporting, do you have to get it verified externally if you also want to say that in your brochures?”
When it comes to ESMA’s Guidelines, part of the concern is legal status, notes Arakelijan. “EmpCo is legislation, while ESMA’s naming rules are guidelines, so it isn’t clear whether a court would give them priority,” she says.
Enforcement questions
A number of regulatory experts within investor bodies have told Responsible Investor that they see little chance of these issues being tested in court. EmpCo was built for physical products, and that would likely be reflected in how it was enforced, they say.
Each EU member state will transpose the directive into national law differently, with some countries handing enforcement powers over to consumer protection agencies and others to competition authorities. Others may leave it to NGOs to go through the courts.
“You need to be located in a country where there’s actually enforcement risk,” says Schmitz, who is based in Germany – arguably the most likely source of EmpCo-based investor litigation because of its big retail market and consumer agencies known to target financial institutions.
But Navin-Jones says investors elsewhere should also be on their guard, because supervisors across the bloc have stated their intention to look into greenwashing in the sector.
In 2023, for example, the Dutch Authority for the Financial Markets (AFM) published its Guidelines on Sustainability Claims, which are broadly in line with EmpCo. It has since done a deep-dive into how pension funds are complying.
A spokesperson told RI the topic “will remain a focus of the AFM in coming years”, adding that any company covered by the UCPD will also soon be covered by EmpCo.
“We expect financial institutions to be aware of this and comply with the rules accordingly,” he said. “We expect market participants to assess their sustainability claims against the applicable legal requirements and the principles set out in our guidelines, and to make further improvements where necessary.”
French supervisor AMF, on the other hand, told RI that EmpCo’s entry into force “is not expected to result in any significant changes for the financial sector” because investors are already subject to the SFDR.
The Danish Financial Supervisory Authority, the Belgian Financial Services and Markets Authority, and Germany’s BaFin have all stepped up their efforts around greenwashing in the investment industry since 2021.
“One of the big questions is whether the consumer protection coordination authorities will act together, with the backing of the Commission, to stop greenwashing in the financial sector through enforcement of the ECGT rules,” says Navin-Jones.
The Commission oversees a group called the CPC Network, which seeks to encourage a harmonised approach to consumer protection by enabling national bodies to cooperate on priority areas, with fines of up to 4 percent of business turnover.
“If the CPC Network targets the finance sector, it will likely drive significant changes across the board,” says Navin-Jones. “If you’ve got all these countries talking about prioritising this issue, it’s logical we might see coordinated action.”
Fund labels
The EmpCo will also affect Europe’s national sustainability fund labels, which are captured by the definition of voluntary labels set out in the regime.

articles.title: Anti Slavery NGO & retail org say: Gig supply chain must do ‘Human rights due diligence’ - cyclingelectric.com
articles.summary: Anti Slavery NGO & retail org say: Gig supply chain must do ‘Human rights due diligence’  cyclingelectric.com
articles.full_text:
Delivery app firms like Deliveroo, Just Eats and Uber Eats, along with major UK supermarkets, are ‘getting off scot-free’ around the potential exploitation of e-mobility reliant delivery riders, say anti slavery campaigners, ahead of a new illegal working ‘code of conduct’ coming into force next week.
From 1 October, a new UK government Code of Conduct will extend Right to Work checks to the gig economy, with any breaches attracting fines of up to £60,000 for each subcontractor working illegally. However, there is no legislation yet requiring that companies tackle modern slavery in their supply chains, only to report on its potential, thus businesses and charities are now calling for even stronger laws. If you’re wondering about the link to electric bikes, it is precisely this business model that has led to a fast expansion of non-road legal products purporting to be ‘e-bikes’, but that are in fact faster than UK regulations allow when fitted. Read on for a clearer explanation.
A spokesperson for Anti-Slavery International told CyclingElectric, ‘with widespread reports of exploitation’ in supermarket supply chains, including among gig workers delivering shopping to customer’s homes, stronger regulation is needed. Both the charity, and the British Retail Consortium are calling for mandatory due diligence to tackle the problem.
Lorcan Jackson-McLaughlin, of Anti-Slavery International, said: “The Government have said illegal working arrests in the UK have doubled in two years, however concerningly the government don’t hold data on the how many of those are identified as potential victims of modern slavery and entered into the national referral mechanism.”
“At the same time, businesses across sectors operating in the UK are getting off scot-free under current supply chain legislation, from supermarkets to platform companies such as Deliveroo.”
“Without legislation mandating that they act, delivery companies will do nothing.”
The British Retail Consortium says while delivery firms and supermarkets have strengthened checks and safeguards against exploitation, the “government needs to do more to tackle labour exploitation at its source by introducing mandatory human rights due diligence.”
Ben Knowles, of cycle logistics firm PedalMe, says a lack of adequate legislation places ethical businesses at a disadvantage. “Anyone in this industry already understands what happens when non-compliant products undercut the legitimate market: we’ve watched it with ‘illegal’ e-bikes for years (which are, legally speaking, not e-bikes at all). The compliant operator can’t meet the price, the customer only sees the headline number, and the honest end of the market either exits or starts cutting corners itself. The same thing is happening in delivery labour, and it’s far less visible because the thing being undercut is a person rather than a product.”
Anti-Slavery International says it will ‘wait and see’ the impact of the new Code of Conduct, known as Schedule 4ZB of the Asylum and Immigration Bill. However, Jackson-McLaughlin warns it would still allow a company to report it “has not taken any steps during the financial year to ensure that slavery and human trafficking is not taking place in its operations or supply chains”.
As the government doesn’t hold data on the levels of illegal working, the true scale of the problem is unknown, at least in the UK. A responsible business conduct review, announced by the Government, is being awaited. Jackson-McLaughlin added: “The time to act is now; the UK has fallen far behind peer countries who have already implemented mandatory due diligence legislation of their own.”
How does exploitation happen and does modern slavery law apply?
French researchers have drawn parallels between the UK and their findings in France, where gig economy delivery cyclists working illegally are almost two-thirds of the workforce.
Of 1,004 delivery app riders in Paris and Bordeaux interviewed by the Santé-Course project, seven out of ten rented accounts from other people, paying around a third of their income to do so. Researcher at the French Institute for Demographic Studies (Ined), Marwân-Al-Qays Bousmah (Qays), said that while he’s unaware of similar surveys in the UK estimating account renting or undocumented worker numbers, given similar gig work structures cross-Channel, “I think we can expect also this situation to happen in the UK.”
Qays and colleagues in the Sante-Course project interviewed riders about their working lives and personal backgrounds. Almost two-thirds (64% of riders), they found, were undocumented in France. Of the 70% of riders renting accounts from others, 20% experienced ‘economic or administrative violence’ – the withholding of funds or of key documentation by account holders.
Qays and his team suggested that account renting in France was conducted by a disparate network of associates, rather than an organised group or gang. While riders might describe these arrangements as positive, the law might term it exploitation. This is depicted in the French language movie Souleymane’s Story, where a friend lets out his delivery account for a cut, before a struggle ensues to access funds earned by the rider.
Researchers found 98.5% of riders were born outside of France and while many were working legally, many weren’t. Qays said: “In my institute, we work a lot with immigrants and immigration. I think it's one of the few sectors in France with the higher share of immigrants than almost all”.
“What we can say at least with our survey is that it's a conservative figure … due to the usual election bias that undocumented people are more afraid to answer.”
Answers to structured questions revealed that after expenses, delivery app riders’ earnings were ‘way below the poverty level’ of €1,228 per month – at just €880 net monthly income. Including waiting time, researchers found, riders worked on average 63 hours per week. 
These far below living wage rates have been confirmed by Cycling Electric as existing in the UK gig economy supply chain and, in part, it is these dire pay levels that drive the trade for non-road-legal, cheap, mass-market kit solutions. These in turn have put pressure on police and fire services.
“In fact, it’s the platforms that, in their public announcements, distort the calculation of working hours by only counting the time between receiving the order and delivery,” said Qays. 
In the UK, Cycling Electric found examples of orders being bundled at source, rather than being treated as separate drops, thus diluting pay rates.
Riders’ perceptions of their own autonomy, and the realities of app-based gig work, often differed. Said Qays: “It is very interesting because they maybe think that they are masters of all their decisions and, of course, in the gig work we know that it's far from the reality”.
“When we speak in general, like ‘do you feel free in meeting your objectives when you work on the platform’, of course they say ‘yes’, but [that’s] compared with working in the construction company with a very hard boss behind them. When we ask really precise questions like, ‘do you feel free to say “no” to a delivery when it pops up on the app’, of course they feel forced to accept because they are afraid to be disconnected afterwards.”
Workers in Edinburgh have called this month on delivery platforms to reveal the decisions made by AI algorithms they claim has reduced their earnings in recent years.
Deliveroo and Uber Eats did not respond to a request for comment to this, nor other stories run by our journalists in this investigation. 
While Just Eat doesn’t operate in France, a Just Eat spokesperson told Cycling Electric it had strengthened Right to Work checks and works with the Home Office to tackle evasion. The spokesperson said: "Just Eat is fully committed to tackling any attempts to provide delivery services illegally via our platform - all couriers must have the right to work in the UK."
In delivery app work, substitute accounts must pre-register in order for Right to Work checks to be carried out, and any new devices logging in must be re-verified. Some delivery companies claim to monitor asylum accommodation hotspots for ‘courier activity’.
Louise Sherry, Sustainability Policy Lead at the British Retail Consortium, said: “Retailers and delivery platforms are committed to upholding high ethical standards across their supply chains and are taking action to address risks. They have been working closely with the Home Office ahead of the expanded Right to Work rules coming into force, with delivery platforms having voluntarily conducted Right to Work checks for several years. EU Backs Carbon Market Changes to Curb Price Spikes
- EU countries agreed to retain surplus carbon permits until 2030, creating a larger buffer that could help contain sharp price increases in the Emissions Trading System.
- The changes follow pressure from Poland, Italy and other governments seeking to limit carbon costs as Europe contends with higher energy prices linked to the Iran conflict.
- The ETS contributes about 11% of industrial electricity bills on average, although the impact varies sharply depending on national power mixes.
European Union countries have backed changes to the bloc’s carbon market that would preserve surplus emissions permits as protection against future price spikes.
EU ambassadors agreed on Wednesday to stop cancelling excess CO2 allowances held in the Emissions Trading System’s Market Stability Reserve, according to diplomats and a draft agreement seen by Reuters.
Instead, the permits would remain available as a supply buffer. The EU could release allowances into the market when carbon prices rise sharply.
The European Commission proposed the changes in April as governments sought ways to contain energy costs following a surge in fuel prices linked to the Iran conflict.
The decision now sets up negotiations with the European Parliament over the final rules.
Building a larger carbon market buffer
The ETS requires major emitters, including power plants and industrial facilities, to buy permits covering their CO2 emissions. Companies can trade allowances, creating a carbon price that fluctuates with market conditions.
The Market Stability Reserve, or MSR, manages excess supply within that system.
Under existing rules, allowances above a specified level in the reserve can be permanently removed. If the MSR contains more than 400 million permits, excess allowances are currently cancelled.
The mechanism also provides protection against rapid price increases. It can release 75 million additional allowances if the EU carbon price more than doubles.
Under the agreement reached by member states, no surplus CO2 permits would be cancelled until 2030.
From 2031, cancellation would resume if the reserve contains more than 800 million allowances. That threshold would then decline each year.
The shift effectively gives policymakers a larger stock of permits that could become available during periods of market stress.
Energy costs put pressure on climate policy
The proposal comes as European governments confront renewed concern over energy affordability and industrial competitiveness.
The ETS is not the primary driver of Europe’s recent energy price increases. However, carbon costs feed into electricity prices, particularly in markets that remain heavily dependent on fossil fuels.
On average, the ETS accounts for about 11% of electricity bills for EU industry. The burden varies considerably across member states.
RELATED ARTICLE: EU Deforestation Law Could Reshape Global Coffee Trade
Countries with fossil fuel-heavy electricity systems, including Poland, face a substantially larger impact. Nations with significant nuclear and renewable generation, such as Sweden, experience a smaller effect.
That disparity has sharpened debate over how the EU should balance carbon pricing with competitiveness and energy security.
Poland and Italy have been among the governments pressing Brussels to limit the ETS contribution to electricity costs.
EU faces a carbon pricing balancing act
For policymakers, the challenge is to introduce greater flexibility without weakening the price incentive at the heart of European climate policy.
The ETS remains the EU’s flagship tool for reducing emissions from power generation and energy-intensive industry. A meaningful carbon price raises the cost of pollution and strengthens the economics of lower-carbon alternatives.
At the same time, volatile prices can create uncertainty for companies making long-term investment decisions. High carbon costs can also compound pressure on manufacturers already exposed to elevated electricity and fuel prices.
Retaining allowances rather than permanently cancelling them gives policymakers another potential tool for managing that volatility. It also changes expectations about future permit supply, an important consideration for carbon traders and regulated companies.
For corporate leaders and investors, the negotiations with Parliament will therefore matter beyond short-term carbon prices. The final design will influence compliance costs, hedging strategies and expectations for future allowance scarcity.
The debate also reflects a wider challenge facing European climate policy. Brussels is trying to maintain credible decarbonisation incentives while protecting industrial competitiveness during another period of energy market disruption.
Member states have now established their negotiating position. The European Parliament will help determine how much flexibility ultimately enters the system, and how the EU balances carbon market stability with its longer-term emissions goals.

Masdar Clean Power Generation Rises 38% as Portfolio Reaches 66.5GW
- Masdar’s operating projects generated 40.2TWh of clean electricity in 2025, up 38%, avoiding 19.5 million tonnes of CO₂e.
- Capacity in operation or under construction climbed about 40% to 45.8GW, while the total global portfolio reached 66.5GW.
- A $1 billion green bond attracted $6.6 billion in orders, with international investors purchasing 85% of the issuance.
Masdar increased clean electricity generation by 38% in 2025 as acquisitions, new projects and construction expanded its global renewable energy footprint.
Operating projects generated 40.2 terawatt-hours (TWh) of clean electricity during the year, compared with 29.2TWh in 2024. The generation helped avoid 19.5 million tonnes of carbon dioxide equivalent, according to Masdar’s 13th Annual Sustainability Report.
Capacity from projects in operation or under construction rose approximately 40%, from 32GW to 45.8GW. Another 20.7GW of secured projects, or projects approaching final investment approval, lifted the company’s total portfolio to 66.5GW by year-end.
Acquisitions broaden Masdar’s European platform
Masdar included Saeta Yield and TERNA ENERGY within its sustainability reporting boundary for the first time in 2025.
The businesses expanded Masdar’s operating presence across Spain, Portugal, Southeastern Europe and Central Europe. Their portfolios add wind and solar assets, alongside a development pipeline that includes pumped hydro storage.
The expansion supports Masdar’s target of reaching 100GW of renewable energy capacity by 2030. It also increases the company’s exposure to markets where grid flexibility and storage are becoming increasingly important as renewable penetration rises.
Mohamed Jameel Al Ramahi, Chief Executive Officer of Masdar, said: “Masdar’s growth reflects the foresight of the UAE’s leadership and the country’s long-term commitment to clean energy. In 2025, our operating projects generated 40.2TWh of clean electricity and avoided 19.5 million tonnes of carbon dioxide emissions, delivering reliable power and tangible economic and environmental benefits for our partners and communities around the world. As we advance towards 100GW by 2030, our focus is not simply on scale, but on building a stronger, more competitive global energy business that continues to create value for the UAE and our partners worldwide.”
Solar, wind and storage projects move forward
Several large projects advanced during the year. The 476MW Baltic Eagle Offshore Wind Farm in Germany began generating power, while Uzbekistan inaugurated the 250MW Nur Bukhara solar project.
Masdar also secured financing for the 2GW Al Sadawi solar project in Saudi Arabia.
In Abu Dhabi, the company broke ground on a gigascale project designed to provide continuous clean electricity. The development combines 5.2GW of solar capacity with a 19GWh battery storage system.
The project is designed to deliver 1GW of clean power around the clock. Its development comes as governments and energy companies examine how large-scale storage can make variable renewable generation more dependable as electricity demand increases.
RELATED ARTICLE: ScottishPower, Masdar Advance $5.4B UK Wind Farm
Green bond demand reaches $6.6 billion
Capital markets remained an important part of Masdar’s expansion strategy.
Following an updated Green Finance Framework published in March, Masdar issued a further $1 billion green bond in May. Orders reached $6.6 billion, making the offering 6.6 times oversubscribed. International investors purchased 85% of the bonds.
The transaction increased Masdar’s outstanding green bonds to $2.75 billion.
The company maintained investment-grade corporate credit ratings of AA- from S&P, A1 from Moody’s and AA- from Fitch. Moody’s also reaffirmed its SQS1, or Excellent, rating for Masdar’s updated Green Finance Framework. Its Sustainable Fitch ESG score increased from 71 to 74 out of 100.
Biodiversity and workforce metrics expand with portfolio
Masdar reported more than 100 community initiatives across eight countries in 2025. It also conducted 23 biodiversity surveys and maintained three conservation partnerships.
At the Zarafshan Wind Farm, AI-powered bird detection technology recorded no fatalities among target species during the reporting period.
Women represented 30.2% of Masdar’s workforce and 20% of management roles. The Emiratization rate stood at approximately 46%, excluding international operations. Employees also completed 250,000 hours of health, safety and environmental training.
For investors and energy executives, Masdar’s 2025 results show how renewable developers are combining acquisitions, project development, storage and green finance to build larger international platforms. The next phase will test whether that growth can translate into reliable generation, disciplined capital deployment and measurable environmental performance as Masdar works toward its 100GW target.

Day 3 at Climate Week NYC: AI, Energy and Climate Delivery
- Subnational governments moved climate policy toward implementation, with California pursuing a carbon-market link with Washington and the Under2 Coalition expanding cooperation on methane, resilience and investment.
- Energy efficiency, electrification and grid modernization dominated business discussions, with leaders arguing that proven technologies now need faster financing and deployment.
- AI’s growing electricity demand entered the climate agenda, as NVIDIA announced an AI Energy Management Coalition with OpenAI and other technology companies.
Climate Week NYC shifted its attention from long-term ambition to the practical machinery of delivery, as governments and business leaders tackled carbon markets, electricity infrastructure, AI demand and industrial efficiency.
Across more than 1,500 events taking place throughout the week, a common challenge emerged. Many technologies needed to cut emissions already exist. The harder task is financing, deploying and integrating them quickly enough to meet climate and energy goals.
That challenge is becoming more urgent as electricity demand grows and governments face pressure to deliver climate policies that also support affordability, jobs and energy security.
States and regions move policy into practice
Subnational governments took a prominent role as governors and ministers from the Under2 Coalition gathered for the inaugural Governors’ Climate Leadership Dialogue and Reception.
California Governor Gavin Newsom also joined Climate Group’s Champa Patel to discuss California’s planned carbon-market linkage with Washington state.
The proposed connection would create a larger carbon market intended to reduce pollution while directing investment toward communities.
The Under2 Coalition and Climate Policy Radar also announced a partnership designed to improve global access to climate laws and policies adopted by states and regions.
Methane was another focus. The Subnational Methane Action Coalition brought government representatives to New York’s Newtown Creek Wastewater Treatment Plant to examine circular-economy approaches. A pilot partnership between CLEE and Maryland will also develop advanced planning and emissions-analysis tools for methane action.
The discussions reflected a broader Climate Week theme: national targets increasingly depend on regional authorities capable of translating commitments into budgets, infrastructure and local policy.
Grid investment becomes an economic priority
Electricity infrastructure emerged as another central issue.
At a McKinsey event, Ernest J. Moniz, founder and CEO of the EFI Foundation, argued that policymakers have yet to build a compelling public case for treating grid modernization as a national priority.
The engineering case may already be established. The political and public narrative remains less developed.
That matters as electrification spreads across transport, buildings and industry while data centers add another source of rapidly growing power demand.
At the Nest Campus, Jigar Shah argued that technologies capable of addressing many data-center energy concerns already exist. The constraint is deployment at sufficient scale.
NVIDIA sustainability chief Josh Parker added another dimension at Climate Forward, announcing a new AI Energy Management Coalition with OpenAI and other technology companies. The initiative will focus on managing AI’s expanding energy requirements.
RELATED ARTICLE: Day 2 at Climate Week NYC: Energy Transition Enters Delivery Era
Efficiency moves from compliance to strategy
Industrial leaders also concentrated on an increasingly immediate question: why are proven efficiency measures still not deployed consistently?
Siemens and the Energy Efficiency Movement used their Twin Engines of Transition sessions to examine efficiency and electrification across industrial systems. Discussions covered existing technologies, financing structures and barriers preventing wider adoption.
The business case is shifting with the energy system. Efficiency can reduce operating costs and exposure to energy volatility while supporting electrification and corporate climate targets.
That places financing at the center of the debate. Companies may have access to workable technologies, but scaling them across factories, buildings and supply chains requires capital and management commitment.
Climate delivery faces a scale test
Climate Week’s message was not confined to technology.
At Climate Forward, actor and activist Jane Fonda highlighted the role of women in climate action, particularly in the Global South.
“Women are among the hardest hit by climate change,” she said, while arguing that women are also leading responses in many affected communities.
The wider significance for executives and investors is increasingly practical. Climate ambition is colliding with electricity demand, infrastructure constraints and capital allocation decisions.
Governments are experimenting with linked carbon markets and regional cooperation. Companies are confronting the energy requirements of AI and electrification. Industrial groups are trying to turn established efficiency technologies into standard business practice.
For global climate goals, the next phase depends less on proving that solutions work and more on whether governments, investors and companies can deploy them at the speed and scale now required.

articles.summary: California and Washington Advance Carbon Market Linkage with NY Climate Week Announcements  ClearBlue Markets
articles.full_text:
On September 23, at New York Climate Week, California Governor Gavin Newsom announced that California is moving ahead with what his office called the next-to-last step in linking its carbon market with Washington State's. Two days earlier, Newsom made the legally required findings that clear the California Air Resources Board (CARB) to begin the formal public rulemaking needed to accept Washington allowances into California's market. Washington Governor Ferguson was also on hand for the announcement and confirmed that state had just finalized its linkage-related rulemaking. The Washington Department of Ecology signed the final version of its updated cap-and-invest rules on September 17, and those rules take effect October 24. Officials continue to target full joint operation sometime in 2027. Quebec representatives were absent from the public announcements, given the upcoming October provincial elections.
“By joining forces with our partner in Washington State, we will build a stronger, more durable carbon market that will drive investment, cut pollution, and power the clean economy,” Newsom said in the announcement. Washington Governor Bob Ferguson struck a similar note: “Linkage isn’t just good climate policy — it’s smart economics. Linking will unlock greater emissions reductions, lower the cost of clean technologies, and create good-paying jobs in high-growth industries.”
The Washington Cap-and-Invest Rulemaking
Washington's Cap-and-Invest Program sets a declining annual cap on the greenhouse gas emissions of roughly 100 of the state's largest polluters, who must buy or receive allowances equal to what they emit. The 2026 rule Ecology adopted on September 17 (effective October 24) locks in changes state lawmakers ordered last year through House Bill 1975, after the program's first two years produced higher and more volatile prices than regulators wanted.
The updated rule holds the price ceiling at a flat USD 80 per allowance for both 2026 and 2027, retroactively enlarges the 2023–2026 emissions budgets by about 6 million metric tons (2.68%) to ease near-term scarcity, and raises how much of each auction a single covered business can buy, from 10% to 25% (with a new, separate 4% cap for financial and other general market participants). The cost containment changes, including the ceiling price, would be aligned with WCI upon linkage. The rulemaking was necessary to facilitate linkage and also to act as an insurance policy to constrain pricing in Washington’s standalone program should linkage be delayed.
It also formally defines a “linkage effective date” as the specific day Washington will start accepting California and Quebec allowances for compliance, and vice versa. Ecology must publicly announce the effective date at least 90 days in advance.
Linkage Means Joint Auctions and a Common Allowance Price
Once linkage takes effect, the jurisdictions will hold joint allowance auctions, with bid lots comprised of a mix of each jurisdiction’s allowance offering. The linkage will lead to a common allowance market price and let companies trade allowances and offset credits freely across every linked jurisdiction. Note, however, prices for offset credits may vary according to individual usage limits and designations. Liquidity will increase. California and Quebec have run this way since their own markets linked on January 1, 2014, and Ontario briefly joined that system before withdrawing in 2018.
Washington, California, and Quebec signed a preliminary linkage agreement on June 25, 2026, but signing that agreement only authorizes the process and doesn't automatically turn linkage on. Each jurisdiction still has to complete its own rulemaking: Washington finished first, with its rule effective October 24. California's is next, with CARB's public rulemaking process now cleared to begin following Newsom's authorization. Quebec's requires a separate rulemaking that becomes final once its linkage agreement is ratified by an Order in Council. Only once all three are done can Ecology, CARB, and Quebec jointly declare the linkage effective date.
What the Market Is Already Pricing In
Washington's allowance prices have had a volatile few years: from a USD 48.50 launch auction in early 2023, prices climbed past USD 70 by the end of 2025 as tight supply and legal challenges to the program kept the market on edge. HB 1975's price ceiling and cap adjustments were designed to calm that volatility, and prices did hold in the low-to-mid USD 60s through the first half of 2026.
Washington's September 2026 quarterly auction settled at just USD 39.50. The surprise settlement came right after California and Quebec wrapped up their own “Program Review” processes to update the Cap-and-Invest and Cap-and-Trade programs. The conclusion of the Program Review clears the runway for each to begin its linkage rulemaking. Secondary-market trading has kept drifting lower since, with Washington's front-December contract closing around USD 38 on September 24.
In contrast pricing in WCI, the linked California-Quebec market, has been soft, trading in a relatively tight band all year and currently around USD 31. Linkage should eventually pull the two prices together into one shared market price. Washington's premium over WCI has been shrinking, as shown on the chart. ClearBlue sees upside for WCI allowance pricing with the rulemaking amendments applying from 2027.
Washington secondary-market allowance prices (front-December contract) vs. the California-Quebec (WCI) secondary spot price, daily, 2026 year-to-date. Source: ClearBlue Markets, Vantage Platform, September 2026.
If California's or Quebec's rulemakings stall, or if the eventual linkage effective date slips well past 2027, Washington's price will keep trading on its own tight fundamentals.

articles.full_text:
UK Pledges $438 Million for Climate Security Risks
- The UK will commit $438 million to address climate and nature-related security risks, including food insecurity, water stress and ecosystem degradation.
- About $437 million will go to the Global Environment Facility, while $1.3 million will support the UN Climate Security Mechanism.
- Britain is pushing for climate and biodiversity risks to be incorporated into national security, intelligence and strategic defence planning.
Britain has pledged $438 million to tackle climate and biodiversity risks that can fuel instability, conflict and economic disruption.
The funding was announced during the UN General Assembly in New York, alongside Climate Week NYC. It forms part of a broader UK effort to reposition environmental disruption as a national security issue rather than solely a climate policy concern.
The government argues that drought, extreme weather, ecosystem degradation and resource scarcity increasingly affect food supplies, migration, financial markets and global supply chains. Those risks can move quickly across national borders.
“Countries need to pool information because a shock beginning in one country can rapidly travel through supply chains, financial markets, and migration patterns to other countries,” UK Foreign Secretary Ed Miliband said.
$437 Million Directed to Global Environment Facility
The largest share of the package, about $437 million, will go to the Global Environment Facility for its 2026-2030 funding period.
The financing will support sustainable agriculture and fishing, food and water security, and resilience to drought and flooding. It will also target environmental degradation, including desertification and deforestation.
Critical ecosystems are another focus. The UK specifically identified forests in the Amazon and Congo Basin among the areas expected to benefit.
A further $1.3 million will go to the UN Climate Security Mechanism. The initiative works with countries to identify climate-related security risks before they contribute to conflict or humanitarian emergencies.
The funding comes from previously announced UK Official Development Assistance allocations.
RELATED ARTICLE: UK, US Link AI Supercomputers for Fusion Research
Climate Risk Moves Into Security Planning
The financial commitment sits alongside a wider diplomatic push from London.
Miliband has called on governments to integrate climate change and ecological degradation into assessments of national security. That includes defence strategies, intelligence systems and strategic military planning.
The approach reflects growing concern that climate shocks can amplify existing geopolitical and economic pressures. Food and water shortages can contribute to displacement and instability, while energy disruptions can expose economies to volatile global commodity markets.
Those vulnerabilities have become particularly visible amid conflict in Iran. Higher oil and gas prices have pushed some countries toward greater coal use, while others have accelerated investment in solar power and electric vehicles.
The result is a more complicated relationship between energy security and decarbonisation. Governments are being forced to manage immediate supply risks while maintaining longer-term climate commitments.
Security Community Ahead of Politics
UK climate transition minister Katie White said security institutions have already spent years incorporating climate threats into their planning.
“The military has been at the forefront of a lot of this climate risk planning for a long time because they’ve always seen that climate change is a threat multiplier,” she said. “The politics is a bit behind the security community on this.”
The UK is seeking to elevate that approach internationally ahead of COP31 in Antalya, Turkey, which begins on November 9.
For companies and investors, the shift broadens the scope of climate risk management. Physical climate risks increasingly intersect with supply-chain resilience, commodity exposure, infrastructure security and geopolitical risk.
That could have implications for corporate scenario planning, investment decisions and disclosures, particularly for businesses dependent on vulnerable agricultural, energy or natural-resource supply chains.
The UK’s $438 million commitment places resilience spending within that wider security framework. It also illustrates how climate finance is increasingly being linked to economic stability and strategic interests.
As governments prepare for COP31, the debate is moving beyond emissions targets alone. Climate resilience, ecosystem protection and national security are becoming more closely connected in both public finance and foreign policy.

The post ESB Raises $575 Million in Ireland’s First European Green Bond Deal appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
ESB Raises $575 Million in Ireland’s First European Green Bond Deal
- ESB raised approximately $575 million through its first European Green Bond, the first Irish corporate issuance under the EU framework.
- The 10-year bond carries a 4.375% coupon, with proceeds directed toward electricity networks, renewable generation and battery storage.
- ESB plans approximately $23 billion of capital investment by 2030 as it expands Ireland’s electricity system and pursues net zero carbon emissions by 2040.
DUBLIN, Ireland: ESB has raised approximately $575 million through its inaugural European Green Bond, becoming the first Irish corporate issuer to use the EU’s regulated green bond format.
The 10-year bond carries a coupon of 4.375%. ESB will allocate the proceeds to eligible investments supporting the decarbonisation and expansion of Ireland’s electricity system.
The transaction is ESB’s fourth green bond but its first under the European Green Bond Regulation. The framework introduces standardised requirements for issuers seeking to label bonds as European Green Bonds.
Capital for Ireland’s electricity transition
ESB plans approximately $23 billion in capital investment by 2030. The programme is designed to build an electricity system capable of supporting housing growth, economic expansion and wider technological change.
The investment aligns with the Irish Government’s National Development Plan and ESB’s strategy to reach net zero carbon emissions by 2040.
Proceeds from the latest bond can finance electricity transmission and distribution infrastructure, renewable electricity generation and battery energy storage systems.
For investors, the structure provides greater visibility into how green bond capital is allocated. That has become increasingly important as sustainable finance markets face greater scrutiny over environmental claims and the use of proceeds.
The issuance follows ESB’s publication of an updated Green Finance Framework and European Green Bond Factsheet in August. Together, the documents establish how green financing proceeds will be allocated and managed.
Moody’s Ratings independently assessed the framework and awarded it its highest sustainability quality score of “Excellent.” Moody’s also completed a pre-issuance review of the European Green Bond Factsheet.
RELATED ARTICLE: Microsoft and ESB Launch Green Hydrogen Pilot to Power Dublin Data Centre
EU rules raise the bar for green finance
The European Green Bond Regulation creates a voluntary standard for issuers seeking to market bonds using the EuGB designation. It aims to improve comparability, transparency and credibility across Europe’s sustainable debt market.
ESB’s decision to issue under the framework places its financing programme within those disclosure and external review requirements.
Anne Marie Kean, ESB Group Treasurer, commented: “The successful completion of ESB’s inaugural European Green Bond is an important milestone in the evolution of our sustainable finance programme. The strong investor support received reflects confidence in ESB’s strategy and our significant investment programme to modernise and expand Ireland’s electricity infrastructure. It also indicates the value that investors put on having a clear and transparent basis for supporting this journey.”
BBVA Corporate & Investment Banking and ING acted as Joint Sustainability Coordinators. They supported ESB in developing its updated Green Finance Framework and European Green Bond Factsheet.
BBVA, Goodbody, ING, MUFG and Société Générale acted as Joint Bookrunners on the issuance.
What investors should take away
The financing comes as electricity grids take a larger role in national climate and economic strategies. Renewable capacity can only expand at scale if transmission, distribution and storage infrastructure develops alongside it.
For ESB, the green bond connects that infrastructure challenge directly with institutional capital. Its planned $23 billion investment programme extends well beyond renewable generation to the networks required to accommodate electrification and growing electricity demand.
The deal also provides an early corporate test of Europe’s new green bond regime. As more issuers consider the EuGB label, investors will gain a clearer view of whether stronger disclosure and external review requirements can establish a more consistent benchmark for sustainable debt.
For Ireland, the capital supports a broader national priority: expanding the electricity system while reducing its carbon intensity. That makes grid investment increasingly relevant not only to climate targets, but also to housing, industrial growth and long-term economic competitiveness.

articles.title: Hong Kong Plans $2.6 Billion Digital Green Bond in World’s Largest Sale
articles.summary:
Hong Kong is preparing a digital green bond sale worth as much as $2.6 billion, potentially setting a new global record for blockchain-based debt issuance. The government is planning an […]
The post Hong Kong Plans $2.6 Billion Digital Green Bond in World’s Largest Sale appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Hong Kong Plans $2.6 Billion Digital Green Bond in World’s Largest Sale
- Hong Kong is preparing to issue up to $2.6 billion in digital green bonds, which would make the transaction the world’s largest digital bond sale.
- The offering will span four currencies, extending Hong Kong’s strategy of combining green finance with blockchain-based issuance and settlement infrastructure.
- Hong Kong plans to make digital bond issuance a regular feature of its capital markets, alongside digital currency settlement and blockchain-based payments and redemptions.
Hong Kong is preparing a digital green bond sale worth as much as $2.6 billion, potentially setting a new global record for blockchain-based debt issuance.
The government is planning an offering worth approximately $1.9 billion to $2.6 billion. The transaction will span four currencies: the U.S. dollar, Hong Kong dollar, euro and offshore yuan.
Investor meetings with financial institutions are taking place this week. Pricing could be determined as early as next Monday.
If completed at the upper end of the proposed range, the deal would strengthen Hong Kong’s position at the intersection of green finance and tokenized capital markets.
Digital bond market scales rapidly
Digital bonds use blockchain technology to manage parts of the issuance, trading and settlement process. For Hong Kong, the technology is becoming part of a broader effort to modernize financial infrastructure while expanding its sustainable finance market.
The government first entered the market in February 2023 with the world’s first government-issued tokenized green bond.
The scale has increased since then. Hong Kong issued approximately $1.3 billion in digital bonds last year. In June, Hong Kong Mortgage Corporation completed a digital bond issuance worth approximately $1.5 billion, setting a global record at the time.
The latest government transaction could exceed that amount.
Settlement infrastructure has also developed. A November 2025 issuance used tokenized central bank digital currency in Hong Kong dollars and yuan for settlement. It attracted approximately $16.7 billion in subscriptions.
The Hong Kong Mortgage Corporation’s June transaction also shortened the settlement cycle from five business days to three.
According to the Hong Kong government, digital bonds issued in the city accounted for approximately half of global issuance from last year through the first half of 2026.
RELATED ARTICLE: Hong Kong Expands Sustainable Finance Taxonomy
Hong Kong builds infrastructure for regular issuance
Chief Executive John Lee has outlined plans to make digital bond issuance a regular government practice. Authorities are also pursuing digital currency settlement and blockchain-based interest payments and redemptions.
The Hong Kong Monetary Authority is building infrastructure to support that shift.
Eddie Yue, Chief Executive of the HKMA, said “this week that Hong Kong had become a hub for global tokenized bond issuance. He said first-half issuance this year represented half of the global total.”
The HKMA plans to support regular government digital bond issuance. It is also preparing a digital asset platform through the Central Moneymarkets Unit, Hong Kong’s bond settlement infrastructure.
The platform is expected to launch by year-end and support settlement using digital Hong Kong dollars.
Authorities also plan to explore connections between tokenized deposits and regulated stablecoins. Another initiative will test the tokenization and management of Exchange Fund bills.
An HKMA spokesperson declined to comment on the planned bond transaction.
Tokenized debt expands across Asia
Hong Kong’s strategy is developing alongside broader experimentation with tokenized financial assets across Asia.
Earlier this month, India’s state-owned REC issued a $59 million digital bond maturing in May 2028. The transaction was India’s first tokenized corporate bond.
Japan is also testing blockchain infrastructure for government debt. Mizuho Financial Group, Nomura Holdings, Japan Securities Clearing Corporation and Digital Asset Holdings began a proof-of-concept in April to digitize Japanese government bond collateral management.
Japan is separately pursuing legislative changes that would allow municipal bonds to be issued as digital securities from April 2027. Taiwan is also advancing real-world asset tokenization, initially prioritizing bonds and gold.
Green finance meets digital capital markets
For investors and financial institutions, Hong Kong’s planned transaction is significant beyond its size. Regular sovereign digital issuance could provide institutional investors with a larger market to test tokenized settlement, custody and liquidity infrastructure.
The green bond structure adds another dimension. It brings sustainable finance into a market increasingly focused on reducing settlement friction and modernizing capital-market infrastructure.
Hong Kong’s proposed $2.6 billion sale would push tokenized debt further into institutional finance. Its wider impact will depend on whether the technology delivers lower costs, greater liquidity and more efficient settlement at scale.
With governments and financial institutions across Asia developing similar infrastructure, Hong Kong is positioning digital green bonds as part of the region’s next phase of capital-market development.

articles.title: The era of unsubstantiated sustainability claims is over as European rules tighten
articles.summary:
As the EU Empowering Consumers Directive approaches enforcement, retailers need technical proof and cross-functional governance to rebuild consumer trust. Consumer trust in retail sustainability claims has hit an all-time low. […]
The post The era of unsubstantiated sustainability claims is over as European rules tighten appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
The era of unsubstantiated sustainability claims is over as European rules tighten
As the EU Empowering Consumers Directive approaches enforcement, retailers need technical proof and cross-functional governance to rebuild consumer trust.
Consumer trust in retail sustainability claims has hit an all-time low. Years of vague marketing slogans and unsubstantiated product labels have left buyers deeply sceptical. The European Union is stepping in to fix this trust deficit. The Empowering Consumers for the Green Transition Directive (EmpCo) establishes a strict regulatory safety net across all B2C consumer sectors. It’s not simply a compliance exercise for retailers but rather a rethink of how they communicate value to their consumer base. Those who view EmpCo as an opportunity to build genuine trust may find themselves with a powerful competitive edge.
Thousands of retailers operating in or selling into the EU market will fall under its scope. If your brand markets products to European consumers, you have to comply before national enforcement begins on 27 September 2026. Ignoring these rules carries severe costs, including financial penalties (which can range from €10,000 to several millions), forced campaign withdrawals and permanent damage to brand reputation. That’s the reality.
EmpCo introduces an outright ban on broad, generic claims like “eco-friendly”, “green” or “sustainable” unless they’re backed by substantiated evidence. The European Commission found that 53% of green claims are vague, misleading or based on unfounded information. It also prohibits carbon-neutrality claims that rely exclusively on carbon offsets outside the value chain.
This directive is designed to improve consumer trust and reward retailers that have been taking action and are transparent about their supply chain. GlobalData’s June 2026 survey found that 48.1% of consumers were sceptical about sustainability communication in the clothing and footwear industry, and 21.3% thought sustainability claims were being used for marketing rather than to achieve a positive environmental impact.
The need for EmpCo isn’t surprising given the wave of greenwashing scandals that have left consumers disappointed and overwhelmed. From fashion retailers making unsubstantiated green collections to food producers exaggerating recycling processes. This directive represents a meaningful step forward, however it also brings new challenges. Faced with the complexity of compliance and risk of penalties, some retailers may retreat into greenhushing. Choosing to remain silent and pivot away entirely from environmental messaging will undermine consumers’ visibility into genuine progress and confidence in the brand.
To meet the requirements, sustainability teams need to collect primary supply chain data across Scope 3 emissions. This means executing rigorous Life Cycle Assessments (LCAs) and Product Carbon Footprints that follow international standards like ISO 14040 and the GHG Protocol. For product-level declarations, Environmental Product Declarations (EPDs) will become the standard requirement for proof.
The good news is most companies will already have detailed data to support their sustainability claims and are actively monitoring it as part of their scope 3 disclosure. They will need to translate highly technical information into digestible messages that are clear and resonate with consumers. The success of this directive will in part rely on effective cross functional cooperation and an aligned framework.
To prepare, retailers must break down internal silos. Historically, marketing teams crafted green campaigns in isolation, while sustainability managers focused on technical reporting. That dynamic isn’t viable anymore.
Retailers need to build a shared claims governance framework to establish credibility:
- Diagnostic audit: Review all active B2C touchpoints such as online product pages, in store displays and packaging to flag generic words or offset-based claims.
- Data integration: Connect procurement and sustainability data streams to verify material origins and recycled content with primary supplier metrics.
- Cross-functional sign-off: Implement mandatory legal, compliance, sustainability and communications review before any new environmental claim goes live to check for accuracy and clarity.
- Verified claims library: Create an internal repository of pre-approved claims backed by audited technical data for marketing teams to use, which should be reviewed on a consistent basis.
The clock is ticking. Physical packaging redesigns and supply chain data collection require lead times of 12 to 18 months. Retailers that delay this process risk getting caught with non-compliant inventory or facing regulatory action.
By embedding technical rigour into everyday communications, retail brands can bridge the gap between sustainability and marketing. Meeting the EmpCo deadline isn’t just a compliance exercise. It’s a strategic opportunity to rebuild genuine consumer trust, protect the brand, and secure a lasting market edge.
Kelly Nugent is a Principal Consultant at South Pole, advising global retail and consumer goods companies on decarbonisation strategy, Scope 3 data substantiation and regulatory compliance.
