Sphera Adds AI Tools to Turn ESG Data Into Business Value
- Sphera is introducing AI-powered sustainability capabilities designed to connect ESG data with operational and financial decision-making.
- New tools target fragmented corporate, supplier and product carbon data as companies navigate changing US and EU disclosure requirements.
- The company argues that sustainability programs tied to business value can remain relevant even as regulatory requirements change.
Sphera is expanding its AI-powered sustainability capabilities as companies face growing pressure to prove the business value of their climate programs.
The sustainability software provider highlighted the new capabilities during Climate Week NYC 2026. Its focus reflects a broader shift in corporate sustainability management. Reporting and regulatory compliance remain important, but executives increasingly expect sustainability teams to demonstrate financial and operational results.
That includes showing how climate initiatives reduce risk, protect revenue and influence capital allocation.
The challenge comes as companies navigate a fluid regulatory environment. California’s SB 253 is reshaping corporate climate disclosure expectations in the US. European sustainability reporting requirements are also evolving.
Sphera argues that programs designed solely around current compliance requirements can become vulnerable when regulations change. By contrast, programs built around measurable business value may prove more resilient.
Breaking down sustainability data silos
A major obstacle is the fragmentation of corporate sustainability data.
Reporting information, supplier metrics and product carbon footprints often sit in separate systems. That makes it harder for executives to determine which initiatives are delivering meaningful results.
Integrating those datasets can provide a clearer view of performance. Companies can assess which supplier partnerships are reducing emissions, which product decisions are lowering footprints and where capital is producing measurable sustainability gains.
Sphera’s new AI capabilities aim to make that process easier.
Within its Corporate Sustainability solution, new functionality supports data collection at the source and seeks to improve data accuracy. It can also map approved information across multiple disclosures.
The goal is to reduce repetitive reporting work while making sustainability data more useful for operational decisions.
For executives, that creates a potential bridge between disclosure and management. The same information used for ESG reporting can help guide investment, procurement and operational priorities.
AI targets product carbon footprint data
Sphera is also rolling out its LCA Automation solution with AI Data Mapping.
The tools focus on improving the quality and consistency of product footprint information. This becomes increasingly important as companies move from calculating individual product footprints to assessing entire portfolios.
Scaling life-cycle assessment can be resource intensive. Companies must collect and standardize large volumes of information across materials, suppliers, manufacturing processes and products.
Automation could help sustainability teams handle that complexity while maintaining consistent methodologies across portfolios.
Better product-level data also carries strategic implications. Companies can use it to compare design choices, engage suppliers and identify emissions hotspots across their value chains.

Linking climate targets with capital decisions
The broader challenge for sustainability teams is translating corporate climate commitments into operational roadmaps.
Sphera’s approach links sustainability objectives with capital spending, supplier engagement and daily business decisions. That connection can help companies identify where climate investments produce measurable operational or financial outcomes.
The theme featured prominently in discussions around Climate Week NYC 2026.
Speaking at the Sustainability Live Leadership Summit, Sphera President and CEO Paul Marushka connected the issue with themes from his book, Sustainable Success: How Businesses Win as a Force for Good.
Marushka told the audience, “Sustainability has reached a new stage of maturity where reporting is no longer the end goal. What matters is driving performance, trust and business value. Sustainability leaders are now measured on business outcomes: risk reduced, revenue protected, capital allocated with confidence and the data required to prove it.”
What executives and investors should watch
For C-suite leaders, the shift raises the stakes around sustainability data governance. Companies need reliable information not only for disclosure, but also for investment and operational decisions.
Investors will likewise need to assess whether corporate sustainability spending translates into measurable outcomes rather than compliance activity alone.
AI can accelerate data collection, mapping and analysis, but governance remains critical. Companies still need controls around data quality, methodologies and accountability for decisions informed by automated systems.
As disclosure rules continue to evolve across major markets, the durability of corporate sustainability strategies may increasingly depend on their connection to business fundamentals. For global companies, climate data is moving beyond the reporting function and deeper into decisions on capital, suppliers, products and risk.

articles.title: Levi Strauss, M&S Launch Fashion Renewable Collaborative
articles.summary:

The post Levi Strauss, M&S Launch Fashion Renewable Collaborative appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Levi Strauss, M&S Launch Fashion Renewable Collaborative
- Fashion manufacturing focus: Textile processing, including fabric mills and dye houses, accounts for more than half of the fashion industry’s emissions.
- Supplier access: The Fashion Renewable Collaborative will support apparel suppliers with PPAs, energy certificates, on-site solar, battery storage and market guidance.
- Industry scale: The initiative builds on a pilot in India that attracted nearly 50 supplier facilities and is now seeking additional fashion brands as sponsors and members.
Levi Strauss & Co., Marks & Spencer and Schneider Electric’s SE Advisory Services have launched the Fashion Renewable Collaborative (FRC), targeting one of fashion’s largest sources of greenhouse gas emissions: electricity used across global manufacturing supply chains.
Announced during New York Climate Week, the program aims to help garment manufacturers, fabric mills and other apparel suppliers access renewable electricity. It will combine education, market guidance and technical support to help suppliers navigate clean energy procurement.
The companies are also inviting other fashion brands to join the initiative. A broader membership could create a more consistent approach to renewable energy procurement across supplier networks that often serve multiple global brands.
Tackling fashion’s manufacturing emissions
Textile processing, including energy-intensive fabric mills and dye houses, accounts for more than half of the fashion industry’s emissions, according to Levi Strauss. Moving these facilities toward renewable electricity is therefore a major opportunity to reduce manufacturing emissions.
Yet suppliers face significant barriers. Renewable electricity can require substantial upfront investment, while energy markets and procurement rules differ across countries. Manufacturers working with several brands can also face conflicting climate requirements.
The FRC is designed to reduce that complexity. Suppliers will receive digital education and market-specific guidance alongside practical support for power purchase agreements, energy certificates, on-site solar and battery storage.
The goal is to replace fragmented brand requirements with a clearer route to renewable electricity procurement.
“It’s become abundantly clear that the most effective way forward on emissions reduction is working in partnership with suppliers. The FRC enables greater support for suppliers that want to access or would like to increase use of renewable electricity but haven’t been able to so far. We can help facilitate adoption while reducing unnecessary duplication,” said Jennifer DuBuisson, senior director of Sustainability at Levi Strauss & Co.
RELATED ARTICLE: Levi Strauss, Schneider Electric Launch Supply Chain Renewable Energy Accelerator in India
India pilot provides model for expansion
The collaborative builds on work already underway within Levi Strauss’ supply chain. The company launched a renewable electricity pilot in India more than a year ago, aimed at improving supplier access to clean power.
Nearly 50 facilities enrolled in the program. Levi Strauss said the participation demonstrated both supplier demand and the importance of reducing barriers to renewable energy adoption.
The FRC will now attempt to apply those lessons across a wider section of the apparel industry.
“It’s a natural extension of work we’ve already been doing with our own suppliers, and we’re glad to bring that experience into this effort with M&S and SE Advisory Services — and ideally more brands in the near future,” DuBuisson said.
That expansion could also have financial implications for participating suppliers. Coordinated procurement and clearer market guidance may help companies assess PPAs and other clean energy investments while avoiding duplicated programs for different customers.
Supply chain decarbonization moves into execution
For Levi Strauss, the initiative forms part of its wider climate transition strategy. The company introduced its Climate Transition Action Plan in 2024, setting a net-zero emissions target for 2050 and a goal to cut supply chain emissions 42% by 2030.
The supply chain accounts for more than 99% of the company’s climate footprint. That places supplier energy use at the centre of its decarbonization strategy rather than at the margins of corporate operations.
For fashion executives and investors, the FRC also illustrates a broader shift in corporate climate programs. Scope 3 targets increasingly depend on whether companies can translate commitments into financing, procurement structures and technical support that suppliers can actually use.
The model could become more consequential if additional brands participate. Suppliers frequently manufacture for several companies at once, making alignment between buyers important for reducing administrative costs and accelerating investment.
As fashion companies work toward 2030 climate targets, renewable electricity in manufacturing is becoming both an emissions issue and a supply chain governance challenge. The FRC is designed to address both by giving suppliers a common framework for turning clean energy targets into projects on the ground.

LEGO Owners Plan $1.6 Billion Climate Investment Push
- KIRKBI Climate plans to invest an additional $1.6 billion over five years, doubling its climate investment portfolio.
- Circular plastics will be a major focus as EU packaging rules increase demand for recyclable materials and recycled content.
- The investor is shifting from thematic investing to active ownership, seeking greater influence over companies as they scale.
The investment arm of the family behind LEGO plans to double its climate portfolio over the next five years, with plastic recycling emerging as a major target for new capital.
KIRKBI Climate currently manages more than DKK 10 billion, or about $1.6 billion. It plans to invest another DKK 10 billion, approximately $1.6 billion, over five years. The strategy will focus on energy transition, circular plastics and land sustainability.
The expansion comes as European regulation begins to change the commercial outlook for recycled plastics. The EU’s Packaging and Packaging Waste Regulation is pushing companies toward more recyclable packaging and greater use of recycled materials.
Yet the economics remain difficult. Recycled plastics must compete against cheaper virgin materials, while fragmented collection and processing systems continue to constrain the sector.
“We can dive in knowing that the market economics don’t work today, but if there’s no chance for the market economics to ever work, then that’s very difficult,” said Anupam Bhargava, CEO of KIRKBI Climate.
Regulation puts plastics in focus
Plastic recycling sits at the intersection of KIRKBI Climate’s investment strategy and Europe’s tightening circular economy rules.
The EU’s packaging regulation creates stronger incentives for companies to redesign packaging, increase recyclability and reduce dependence on virgin materials. That policy backdrop could improve demand for technologies capable of producing recycled plastics at scale.
For investors, however, regulation alone does not remove the commercial risks.
Recycling infrastructure remains uneven across Europe. Feedstock quality can vary, while virgin plastic prices can make recycled alternatives less competitive. Scaling recycling technologies therefore requires both patient capital and clearer routes to commercially viable demand.
KIRKBI Climate plans to concentrate its recycling investments on plastics and selected European markets. Future capital will be broadly divided between recycling and energy.
RELATED ARTICLE: LEGO Raises Carbon Removal Commitment to $7.9Million
KIRKBI shifts from investor to active owner
The strategy also changes how the family-backed investor intends to deploy capital.
KIRKBI Climate is moving from thematic investment toward active ownership. It plans to take positions large enough to exert meaningful influence at board level and help companies build operations and scale technologies.
The company has strengthened its leadership team to support that shift.
Lars Villadsen has been appointed CFO and COO. He brings more than 20 years of experience spanning finance, operations and energy transition investments. His previous roles include co-founding Glentra Capital and spending 12 years at Vestas, including seven as CFO for North America.
Emma Nehrenheim will become Head of Energy Transition. She currently serves as Managing Director of the European Battery Alliance and Strategic Leader for the Battery Portfolio at EIT InnoEnergy. She previously spent eight years at Northvolt, including leading its Revolt recycling business.
Nehrenheim will join on November 1, followed by Villadsen on December 1.
“We are transforming KIRKBI Climate from an investor to a business builder, taking active ownership to scale companies that deliver real climate impact. Lars and Emma bring exactly the financial, operational and technical experience we need to put that strategy into action, as we help tackle some of the world’s toughest climate challenges.”
Long-term capital targets difficult climate sectors
KIRKBI Climate was established in 2025 to consolidate the Kirk Kristiansen family’s climate-focused investments. It sits within KIRKBI, the family-owned holding company behind the LEGO Group and other investments.
Its approach combines investment in proven technologies with longer-term backing for emerging solutions that require capital to reach commercial scale.
For executives and investors, the plastics strategy highlights how regulation can reshape capital allocation before underlying market economics fully mature. Europe’s packaging rules are creating stronger demand drivers, but recycling companies must still prove that their technologies can compete on cost, quality and scale.
KIRKBI Climate’s planned $1.6 billion expansion puts long-term family capital behind that transition. Its shift toward active ownership also shows a willingness to take operational risk, not simply financial exposure, as Europe builds a more circular plastics economy.

articles.title: CPI Research Finds Latin America Climate Finance Doubled
articles.summary:
Climate finance across Latin America and the Caribbean has doubled in four years, but capital is still falling short of the region’s transition needs. New research from Climate Policy Initiative […]

articles.full_text:
CPI Research Finds Latin America Climate Finance Doubled
- Climate finance across Latin America and the Caribbean reached $108 billion in 2024, doubling from $54 billion in 2020.
- Fossil fuel investment still reached $95 billion, more than twice the $43 billion in climate finance directed to energy systems.
- Adaptation attracted just 11% of tracked climate finance, while major funding gaps persist across transport, industry and land use.
Climate finance across Latin America and the Caribbean has doubled in four years, but capital is still falling short of the region’s transition needs.
New research from Climate Policy Initiative (CPI) found climate finance reached $108 billion in 2024, up from $54 billion in 2020. The growth comes as renewables already provide close to 60% of regional electricity, more than twice the global average.
Yet the broader capital picture remains heavily exposed to fossil fuels. Around $95 billion flowed into fossil fuels in 2024. By comparison, climate finance for energy systems totaled $43 billion.
The figures suggest that closing the transition gap will require more than mobilizing new money. Governments and financial institutions will also need to redirect existing capital toward low-carbon and climate-resilient investment.
“Climate finance in Latin America and the Caribbean (LAC) has doubled. The key question now is whether finance is reaching the investments that can drive the region’s climate transition while delivering broader economic and development benefits,” said Barbara Buchner, Chief Executive Officer, Climate Policy Initiative. “The region has significant pools of domestic capital, growing private-sector interest, and major investment opportunities across energy, transport, agriculture, and nature. The priority now is to mobilize funding at scale, by reducing barriers to investment and better connecting available finance with bankable opportunities.”
Critical sectors remain short of capital
Despite the four-year increase, climate finance was broadly flat against 2023, when flows reached about $110 billion.
Some of the largest gaps sit in sectors central to decarbonization. Industry receives roughly 26 times less climate finance than estimated mitigation needs through 2030. Transport receives around 25 times less.
Agriculture, forestry and other land use receives more than seven times less than estimated regional needs. Excluding Brazil, that gap rises to 125 times. This is particularly significant because the sector accounts for 54% of LAC greenhouse gas emissions.
The economic case for closing these gaps extends beyond emissions. CPI estimates the climate transition could generate more than $15 trillion in economic co-benefits through 2050. That equates to roughly $577 billion annually, more than five times the climate finance tracked in 2024.
Fossil fuels compete for investment
The region starts with a comparatively clean electricity system. Renewables account for around 60% of its power mix, with hydropower supplying about half of clean generation.
However, hydropower dependence also exposes electricity systems to drought and climate variability. That raises the investment case for diversified renewables, grids, storage and resilience.
Fossil fuels remain a major competitor for capital. The $95 billion invested in fossil fuels during 2024 was more than double climate finance for energy systems.
Redirecting part of those financial flows could therefore complement efforts to raise new transition capital. The region also has opportunities across critical minerals, forests, biodiversity and other natural assets.
RELATED ARTICLE: Salesforce Unveils Sustainable AI Policy Principles and Climate-Focused Initiatives
Domestic finance provides a foundation
Local capital already plays a substantial role. Domestic sources supplied around 69% of tracked climate finance in 2023 and 2024.
Brazil accounted for 58% of LAC climate finance in 2024, with domestic actors providing around 90% of its total. Climate finance in Brazil has grown at a 28% compound annual rate since 2020, driven largely by solar installations and climate-aligned agriculture.
Mexico receives around 64% of its climate finance domestically. Central America has also increased its domestic share, from roughly 10% in 2021 and 2022 to 34% in 2023 and 2024.
Private capital, however, remains concentrated in mature markets. Outside Brazil, Mexico and Chile, public actors provided between 60% and 84% of climate finance in 2023 and 2024.
Adaptation trails mitigation
Adaptation remains one of the clearest financing weaknesses. It accounted for only 11% of tracked climate finance in 2023 and 2024, reaching $12.5 billion last year.
Mitigation finance reached $85 billion in 2024 and has more than doubled since 2020. Adaptation finance increased by 56% over the same period.
That imbalance leaves infrastructure, agriculture, energy systems and businesses increasingly exposed to physical climate risks.
CPI points to high capital costs, political and macroeconomic volatility, fragmented regulation and weak project pipelines as persistent barriers. It calls for stronger investment roadmaps, guarantees, local-currency solutions, project aggregation and climate-risk integration.
For investors and executives, the central issue is increasingly capital allocation. LAC already has substantial domestic finance, deep renewable resources and growing sustainable finance markets. Turning those advantages into investable projects will determine whether the region can convert rising climate finance into a broader economic transition.

articles.summary:
Climate Week NYC discussions moved beyond whether the global transition will happen and focused increasingly on how quickly governments and businesses can deliver it. Energy, industry, food systems, artificial intelligence […]

articles.full_text:
Day 2 at Climate Week NYC: Energy Transition Enters Delivery Era
- Energy and investment: Leaders called for faster electrification, renewable deployment and efficiency as electricity demand rises from AI, data centres and industrial growth.
- Industry and supply chains: Steel, cement, food and manufacturing discussions shifted toward procurement, traceability and creating demand for lower-carbon materials.
- Climate governance: Governments, companies and investors face growing pressure to turn targets into projects, financing and infrastructure that deliver benefits locally.
Climate Week NYC discussions moved beyond whether the global transition will happen and focused increasingly on how quickly governments and businesses can deliver it.
Energy, industry, food systems, artificial intelligence and climate finance dominated conversations. Across them ran a common theme: technologies increasingly exist, but deployment, capital and policy are struggling to keep pace.
Dr. Fatih Birol, Executive Director of the International Energy Agency, described the world as entering an age of electricity. Yet the pace of change needs to double.
For climate-vulnerable countries, that timeline carries much higher stakes. Dr. Maina Vakafua Talia, Climate Minister of Tuvalu, put the consequences plainly. “For us, it’s a matter of life and death.”
Investment moves from targets to projects
Several announcements showed the scale of capital now being sought for the transition.
Lagos State unveiled a $25 billion to $50 billion pipeline containing more than 300 investment-ready projects. Five governments also backed the new Blend Better Cement campaign.
L’Oréal opened the second cohort of its €100 million L’AcceleratOR program to 13 companies. AstraZeneca launched CARESA, a free tool designed to measure the environmental footprint of patient care.
Industrial decarbonisation featured heavily. Steel buyers and suppliers discussed how procurement standards can create demand for cleaner production. Cement discussions focused on blended products that reduce clinker use and can support more localised supply chains.
The message for investors was increasingly practical. Capital needs credible standards, transparent supply-chain data and sufficient demand to make lower-carbon production commercially viable.
AI puts electricity demand under scrutiny
Artificial intelligence emerged as both a climate tool and a new source of infrastructure pressure.
Manufacturers are already applying AI to energy management, equipment and building systems. Trane Technologies said autonomous building controls can generate substantial efficiency improvements from existing equipment.
The larger debate concerned data centres. Their rapid expansion is increasing scrutiny of electricity use, grid capacity, water demand and relationships with host communities.
Speakers argued that efficiency must develop alongside new generation. Waste heat could also become a resource where cities, data centres and nearby buildings can establish the infrastructure needed to reuse it.
RELATED ARTICLE: Day 1 at Climate Week NYC: Leaders Shift Focus to Delivery
Kate Gallego, Mayor of Phoenix, captured the growing expectations facing developers. “Cities are open for business, but not for sale.”
For executives, the implication is that access to power alone may no longer determine where digital infrastructure gets built. Water, grid resilience, community impact and local economic benefits are becoming part of the investment equation.
Food and materials move up the climate agenda
Food systems were another major focus. Speakers estimated they account for roughly one-third of greenhouse gas pollution, while debates ranged from regenerative agriculture to traceability and consumer behaviour.
The discussion challenged the idea that sustainable consumption depends mainly on individual choice. Price, availability, agricultural subsidies and government policy all influence what consumers ultimately buy.
Similar questions surfaced around steel and cement. Buyers increasingly want supplier-specific emissions information rather than broad industry averages. Public procurement can reinforce that demand through specifications and environmental product declarations.
The broader challenge is creating markets where lower-carbon production is rewarded rather than penalised by higher upfront costs.
Climate strategy enters a harder phase
The closing discussions reflected a transition that is becoming more economically and politically complex.
Former Australian Prime Minister Kevin Rudd pointed to renewables, electrification, AI and China as four areas central to the next phase of climate action.
Meanwhile, International Energy Agency analysis presented at the event placed electricity at the centre of the changing global energy system.
The question for corporate leaders is therefore shifting. Setting a target is increasingly only the starting point.
The next phase will depend on securing power, financing infrastructure, strengthening supply chains and demonstrating value to the communities hosting new investment.
As governments and businesses compete for capital in that transition, the dividing line may increasingly be execution: who can convert climate ambition into investable projects, resilient infrastructure and measurable economic outcomes fastest.

articles.full_text:
Day 1 at Climate Week NYC: Leaders Shift Focus to Delivery
- Nigeria launched a $300 million clean energy fund, while new initiatives targeted freight decarbonization and the use of AI in climate action.
- Grid capacity emerged as a central concern as data centers, transport electrification and clean energy compete for infrastructure and power.
- Leaders pushed for faster implementation of existing technologies, arguing that finance, policy and infrastructure now matter as much as innovation.
Climate Week opened with a message that cut across government, business and civil society: much of the technology needed for the energy transition already exists. The harder task is deploying it quickly, affordably and at scale.
That challenge ran through discussions on renewable energy, artificial intelligence, transport, industrial decarbonization, methane and government resilience.
It also produced immediate commitments. Nigeria launched a $300 million clean energy fund focused on expanding access to off-grid power. Türkiye’s COP31 delegation announced a global initiative exploring how artificial intelligence can support climate progress.
Climate Group’s EV100 also announced a partnership with Smart Freight Centre. The initiative will target freight decarbonization, beginning in Mexico and South Africa.
Helen Clarkson OBE, CEO of Climate Group, framed the consequences of delayed action in stark terms. “Silence isn’t neutral, it’s dangerous. Silence enables inaction, and inaction leads to more climate change. More flooding, more fires, more empty supermarket shelves, more pollution, more uninsurable homes.”
Power demand puts grids under pressure
The collision between rising electricity demand and aging grid infrastructure emerged as one of the day’s clearest business risks.
BloombergNEF’s Stephanie Diaz said data centers are on course to add 118 GW of demand to the US grid by 2030. They could account for around 12% of average US electricity demand by then and roughly one-fifth by 2035.
That expansion is forcing utilities, technology companies and policymakers to confront questions about where new data centers are built and how they are powered.
PG&E Chief Sustainability Officer Aaron Johnson argued that existing infrastructure has more flexibility than headline capacity figures suggest. “The electric grid is only used 45% of the time.”
Congestion tends to occur during limited periods, creating opportunities for batteries, better software and smarter siting of large electricity users. However, equipment shortages and manufacturing constraints remain significant barriers to rapid grid expansion.
The same challenge is appearing in transport. Speakers called for charging infrastructure to become part of grid planning rather than arriving after electric vehicle demand materializes.
Uruguay provided evidence of how quickly adoption can change electricity needs. Seven in ten new vehicles sold there in August were fully electric, according to figures cited during the event.
RELATED ARTICLE: Climate Week NYC Opening Ceremony: Key Principles for Climate Action—Who, What & Why
Investment shifts toward implementation
Across the sessions, speakers repeatedly returned to the gap between available capital and investable projects.
India offered one example of how policy can narrow that divide. The country has expanded non-fossil power capacity roughly fourfold since 2014, according to speakers from the International Solar Alliance and Indian government.
Policy measures have reduced project risk and improved bankability for international investors. Corporate demand is also playing a growing role in supporting renewable deployment.
Yet supply-chain concentration remains a concern. Clean energy manufacturing continues to cluster in relatively few markets, exposing developers to geopolitical and trade risks.
Energy efficiency received similar attention. Executives argued that governments should treat efficiency alongside generation and transmission when planning future energy systems. Existing motors, cooling equipment and building technologies can reduce demand without waiting for major technological breakthroughs.
Climate policy meets economic and political reality
The discussions also moved beyond technology.
Government resilience, industrial jobs and public support featured prominently as leaders considered how climate policy can survive tighter budgets and political uncertainty.
A new Apolitical survey presented during the event found that only one in six public servants believes their government is prepared for coming climate impacts. The findings accompanied the launch of a government resilience campus aimed at strengthening public-sector capacity.
The transition’s impact on workers was another recurring theme. Speakers from labor, government and environmental organizations argued that industrial policy must pair decarbonization with well-paying employment and stronger domestic supply chains.
Rwanda’s Environment Minister Bernadette Arakwiye captured the broader implementation challenge: “True partnership requires an implementable plan, clarity on roles, and accountability. It has to deliver results on the ground.”
That may be the clearest takeaway from Climate Week’s opening discussions. Governments and companies are no longer debating only which technologies can cut emissions.
The harder questions concern who finances them, where infrastructure gets built and whether grids can accommodate rapidly changing demand. For executives and investors, execution risk is increasingly becoming climate strategy itself.

articles.title: Grassroots Carbon Targets 40 Million U.S. Acres by 2030
articles.summary:
Grassroots Carbon has set a goal to expand its work across 40 million acres of U.S. grazing land by 2030, taking a major bet on regenerative grazing and environmental markets. […]

articles.full_text:
Grassroots Carbon Targets 40 Million U.S. Acres by 2030
- Grassroots Carbon plans to support improved grazing management across 40 million acres of U.S. grazing land by 2030, equal to roughly 6% of the national total.
- At least 10 million acres are expected to be fully verified through recognized pathways as part of the One Billion Acres campaign.
- The company says corporate investment in measured carbon, water and biodiversity outcomes could create new revenue for ranchers while financing more resilient agricultural operations.
Grassroots Carbon has set a goal to expand its work across 40 million acres of U.S. grazing land by 2030, taking a major bet on regenerative grazing and environmental markets.
Announced during Climate Week NYC, the target would expand the company’s reach more than thirteenfold. Grassroots Carbon currently works with 340 ranching families across 22 states and approximately 3 million acres.
At least 10 million acres under the 2030 ambition will be fully verified through recognized pathways. That commitment forms part of One Billion Acres, the impact campaign for Groundswell.
The broader 40-million-acre target is equivalent to roughly 6% of U.S. grazing lands. The U.S. Department of Agriculture estimates the country has approximately 659 million acres of grassland pasture and range.
From carbon markets to ranch economics
Grassroots Carbon began in 2021 with 10 ranching families in Texas, known internally as the “Texas 10.” Its model seeks to connect ranchers implementing improved grazing management with companies willing to pay for measured environmental outcomes.
The company currently delivers verified increases in soil organic carbon from atmospheric carbon drawdown. It also measures greenhouse gas reductions linked to changes in management and inputs, including nitrogen fertilizer.
Programs covering water and biodiversity outcomes are also under development. These include volumetric water benefits and improvements in habitat and grassland bird populations.
For Grassroots Carbon, however, environmental credits are intended to support the economics of the underlying agricultural business.
“We’re not trying to turn ranches into carbon projects. We’re trying to help ranching families build better businesses on healthier, more productive land.”
Improved grazing management can increase grass availability and grazing days, according to the company. It can also help reduce certain input costs and improve resilience to drought, heat, wildfire and erosion.
Scaling without sacrificing verification
The expansion highlights a persistent challenge for nature and agricultural markets: how to increase participation while maintaining credible measurement.
Grassroots Carbon physically samples soil to a depth of one meter rather than relying exclusively on modeled or practice-based estimates. It also documents changes in grazing management.
The company argues that rigorous standards remain essential for corporate buyers seeking defensible environmental claims. Independent verification can also protect ranchers whose practices underpin those claims.
But verification can take years, creating tension between the pace of environmental measurement and the financing needed to change agricultural practices.
“We should not have to choose between rigor and scale.”
Grassroots Carbon wants systems that allow ranchers to begin transitions, attract capital and build evidence for verification over time. The company maintains that this should not require weakening environmental standards.
For corporate buyers, that issue is becoming increasingly important as scrutiny of environmental claims intensifies. Companies purchasing nature-related outcomes need evidence that can withstand investor, regulatory and stakeholder examination.
RELATED ARTICLE: Grassroots Carbon Reaches 1.9 Million Tons of Verified Soil Removals for Net Zero Demand
Putting management at the center
Grassroots Carbon is also challenging broad assumptions about livestock’s environmental footprint by focusing on land management.
“A cow is not a management practice.”
The company argues that grazing outcomes depend heavily on how cattle are moved and how long land is allowed to recover. Managed grazing can stimulate plant growth, improve ground cover and support nutrient cycling. Under suitable conditions, deeper root systems may also improve water retention and carbon storage.
That distinction matters for investors and companies considering agricultural climate strategies. Rather than certifying ranches, animals or products as “regenerative,” Grassroots Carbon measures specific environmental outcomes associated with management changes.
It also places ranchers at the center of the model. Those operators may need to install fencing and water infrastructure, change herd rotations or allow longer pasture recovery periods before benefits become apparent.
Corporate capital meets working lands
Reaching 40 million acres will require considerably more corporate participation. Grassroots Carbon cited Nestlé among companies that have already invested alongside its programs.
Long-term demand could provide ranchers with additional revenue while directing private capital toward soil health and agricultural resilience. For companies, the model offers access to measured environmental outcomes tied directly to working U.S. landscapes.
The scale remains ambitious. Grassroots Carbon must move from approximately 3 million acres today to 40 million within four years.
“The limitations of today’s systems should not define what we believe is possible tomorrow.”
Whether that expansion can maintain verification standards will be central to its credibility. The wider question reaches beyond one company. If environmental markets can connect corporate demand with measurable improvements on working lands, U.S. grazing country could become a larger destination for private climate and nature finance.
For companies and investors, the opportunity is not simply carbon. It is whether credible environmental measurement can turn land stewardship into durable economic value while strengthening the resilience of the rural businesses managing that land.

Navitas Solar Plans $1 Billion Clean Energy Expansion
- Navitas Solar plans to invest $1.04 billion over five years across Gujarat and Maharashtra, expanding from solar modules into cells, wafers, ingots, storage and power generation.
- A 2.4 GW solar cell facility is already under development in Gujarat, with its first phase expected to begin operations by July 2027.
- The expansion also includes a 5 GWh battery storage facility and two solar parks, strengthening Navitas Solar’s position across the clean energy value chain.
Navitas Solar plans to invest $1.04 billion over the next five years to build a more integrated clean energy business across Gujarat and Maharashtra.
The privately owned Indian solar manufacturer will expand beyond its existing module operations into upstream manufacturing, battery storage and renewable power generation. The investment covers solar ingots, wafers, cells and modules, alongside new energy storage and generation capacity.
The strategy would give Navitas greater control across the solar supply chain at a time when India is pushing to expand domestic clean energy manufacturing.
Building an integrated solar supply chain
Navitas currently has 3 GW of annual solar module manufacturing capacity. Its next phase will move the company further upstream into the components required to manufacture those modules.
A major part of that expansion is already underway in Sisodara, Gujarat. Navitas is developing a 2.4 GW solar cell manufacturing facility there.
The first phase will involve approximately $125 million of investment and is targeted to begin operations by July 2027.
Adding cell production creates a more vertically integrated manufacturing structure. Planned investments in ingots and wafers would extend that integration further upstream.
For solar manufacturers, greater control over these production stages can reduce exposure to external suppliers and improve oversight of costs, quality and availability. It can also support India’s wider effort to build more domestic manufacturing capacity across the renewable energy supply chain.
The scale of the Navitas investment also reflects how manufacturers are broadening their strategies as India’s renewable energy market grows. Companies increasingly face demand not only for generation equipment, but also for technologies that can support grid reliability.
Battery storage joins the expansion
Navitas plans to add battery energy storage to its portfolio through a 5 GWh facility in Vadodara, Gujarat.
The move takes the company beyond solar manufacturing and into one of the technologies increasingly viewed as critical to renewable power systems.
Battery storage can absorb electricity when renewable generation is high and release it when required. That capability becomes increasingly important as grids integrate larger volumes of variable solar and wind power.
For Navitas, the planned facility creates another business line alongside its solar manufacturing operations. It also positions the company across both renewable energy production and the infrastructure needed to manage that electricity.

Maharashtra projects extend into generation
The five-year strategy also includes direct renewable power generation.
In Maharashtra, Navitas is developing two solar parks with capacities of 200 MW and 25 MW. These projects extend the company’s presence beyond manufacturing into renewable energy assets.
Taken together, the investments create a business spanning several stages of the clean energy value chain. Navitas would have exposure to upstream solar materials, cells, modules, battery storage and electricity generation.
That breadth could become increasingly relevant as India’s power system expands renewable capacity and seeks stronger domestic supply chains.
India’s clean energy manufacturing race accelerates
India has been working to increase domestic production of solar equipment while reducing reliance on imported components. Expanding local manufacturing has become closely tied to the country’s industrial, energy security and climate priorities.
For investors and corporate energy buyers, the growth of integrated domestic manufacturers could influence equipment availability, project economics and supply-chain risk.
The addition of storage is equally significant. Renewable deployment increasingly depends on investment in grids, storage and other flexibility technologies alongside new generation capacity.
Navitas Solar’s $1.04 billion plan brings those elements together under one expansion strategy. If delivered as planned, the company will move from a primarily module-focused manufacturer toward a broader clean energy platform.
That shift reflects a wider transformation underway across India’s renewable energy sector. Manufacturing scale remains important, but the next phase of competition is increasingly about controlling more of the value chain while building the infrastructure needed to support a larger, more flexible clean power system.

Barclays Appoints Paul Williams as Global Head of Operational Sustainability
- Barclays has appointed Paul Williams as Global Head of Operational Sustainability, expanding senior leadership around the bank’s sustainable operations strategy.

- The appointment brings sustainable procurement expertise into a broader operational remit as banks face growing scrutiny over supply chains, real estate, technology and environmental performance.
Barclays has appointed Paul Williams as its new Global Head of Operational Sustainability, placing him in charge of sustainability strategy across several of the bank’s core operational functions.
Williams will lead the bank’s sustainable operations strategy and work to embed sustainability across Procurement, Global Real Estate, Technology and wider business operations. His remit will support Barclays’ strategic commitments, regulatory requirements and longer-term sustainability objectives.
The appointment puts operational sustainability at the intersection of areas that carry significant environmental, financial and governance considerations for global banks. These range from supplier standards and property portfolios to technology infrastructure and broader corporate operations.
From sustainable procurement to bank-wide operations
Williams joins Barclays from Deutsche Bank, where he has served as Global Head of Sustainable Procurement since 2024.
His work there focused on integrating sustainability considerations into procurement and translating corporate sustainability ambitions into practical action across supplier relationships.
Before Deutsche Bank, Williams served as Global Head of Environmental & Social Sustainability at international food and beverage group Princes Limited.
He is also the founder and chair of the Finance Initiative for Sustainable Procurement (FISP). The collaboration brings together financial services institutions seeking to improve sustainability performance across shared supply networks.
That experience gives Williams a background spanning both corporate sustainability and procurement. At Barclays, his responsibilities will extend beyond sourcing into real estate, technology and other operational areas.
Announcing the move, Williams wrote:
“A new chapter begins…
After what has been an incredibly rewarding period at Deutsche Bank, I’m excited to share that I have moved into a new role at Barclays as Global Head of Operational Sustainability.”
Reflecting on his previous role, he added:
“There have been some fantastic experiences and achievements during my time — from developing and embedding sustainable procurement approaches, to working with colleagues, suppliers and industry peers to turn sustainability ambitions into practical action.”

Sustainability moves deeper into bank operations
For financial institutions, sustainability strategy increasingly reaches beyond financed emissions and capital allocation. The operational side of banking also brings exposure to supply chain standards, energy use, buildings, technology and procurement practices.
Williams’ remit reflects that wider scope. Bringing Procurement, Global Real Estate and Technology into an operational sustainability strategy creates a framework for addressing environmental considerations across functions that account for significant corporate spending and supplier relationships.
It also has a governance dimension. Sustainability requirements can affect procurement controls, supplier oversight and operational decision-making, particularly as financial institutions respond to evolving regulatory expectations across jurisdictions.
Williams said:
“In my new role, I’ll be leading the sustainable operations strategy, embedding sustainability across Procurement, Global Real Estate, Technology and wider business operations.”
He will take over responsibilities previously handled by Anna Long, who Williams said had been “double hatting over recent months.”
What executives and investors should watch
The appointment comes as large financial institutions face pressure to demonstrate how sustainability commitments translate into day-to-day corporate decisions. For executives, that creates a need for clearer accountability across functions traditionally managed separately from sustainability teams.
Procurement is particularly relevant because major banks rely on extensive networks of technology, professional services, property and other suppliers. Embedding sustainability criteria into these relationships can influence operational emissions, supplier engagement and risk management.
Real estate and technology add further dimensions, from energy use in offices and data infrastructure to decisions about equipment, services and facilities.
For investors, the practical test will be execution. Leadership appointments can establish accountability, but progress ultimately depends on how sustainability objectives influence procurement standards, investment decisions and operational performance.
Williams said he is now “very excited for the new adventure ahead and collaborating with the many people across Barclays who will be part of the journey.”
His move reflects a broader challenge facing global finance: turning high-level sustainability commitments into decisions embedded across the machinery of large organisations. For banks operating across multiple markets and regulatory regimes, that operational layer is becoming an increasingly important part of sustainability governance.

Day 4 at Climate Week NYC: Governments and Business Focus on Climate Delivery
- Governments pushed cross-border climate delivery: Governors and ministers from across the Americas focused on electrification, resilience, clean industry and investment through the Under2 Coalition.
- Buildings moved to the centre of implementation: The Empire State Building provided a live case study for energy efficiency, electrification and lower-carbon retrofits in existing urban assets.
- Climate communication widened its audience: Insurance costs, sport and information integrity emerged as ways to connect climate risk with everyday economic and social concerns.
By Day 4 of Climate Week NYC, one theme was cutting across boardrooms, government meetings and public forums: climate action increasingly depends on how effectively institutions can turn existing solutions into practical delivery.
Across New York, discussions moved from solar investment and building efficiency to sport, insurance and public trust. The breadth reflected a climate agenda expanding beyond emissions targets alone.
For executives and investors, the focus was increasingly practical. Capital, policy coordination, credible communication and implementation capacity are becoming central to whether climate commitments translate into economic change.
Governments look beyond borders
The Under2 Coalition and the Government of Québec brought governors and ministers from across the Americas together to examine cross-border climate cooperation.
Electrification, resilience, clean industry and investment were central to the discussion. The meeting reflected the growing role of subnational governments in climate implementation, particularly where national politics or regulatory systems move at different speeds.
Elsewhere, the Indonesia Solar Investment Forum put financing at the centre of the energy transition.
Government, investors and industry representatives examined what Indonesia needs to finance solar deployment at scale. Participants included RE100, the Indonesia Solar Energy Association, S&P Global and the Columbia Center on Sustainable Investment.
The discussion highlighted a challenge facing many emerging markets. Renewable technologies are increasingly established, but deployment still depends on bankable projects, supportive regulation and access to capital.
Buildings become a test of climate execution
Inside the Empire State Building, Climate Group’s Smart Energy team turned attention to the built environment.
Its Global Policy Working Group examined energy-efficiency policy, including Minimum Energy Performance Standards. The discussion focused on how governments can strengthen efficiency requirements and accelerate improvements across existing building stock.
The building itself provided the case study.
The Empire State Building has undergone extensive work around efficiency and electrification while remaining an occupied, landmarked property. Corgan’s office on the 54th floor offers another example. Its renovation sought to reduce material use and select products with lower global warming potential.
The office is also pursuing Zero Carbon Certification from the International Living Future Institute.
For property owners and corporate occupiers, the implications extend beyond operational emissions. Building performance increasingly intersects with asset value, regulation, energy costs and corporate climate targets.
RELATED ARTICLE: Day 3 at Climate Week NYC: AI, Energy and Climate Delivery
Climate risk becomes personal
At the Associated Press offices, discussions shifted from climate technology to climate communication.
Eric Asche of the Potential Energy Coalition argued that communicators should begin with concerns people already share. Insurance offered a particularly immediate example as climate-related risks increasingly intersect with household finances.
“I don’t want my neighbors’ insurance cost to go up, and I certainly don’t want my insurance to go up.”
Another session examined why climate communications can struggle to connect with wider audiences. Participants pointed to moral framing, excessive emphasis on distant future impacts and a reluctance to experiment with approaches that could fail.
The broader question is becoming more important as climate policy reaches deeper into daily economic life. Public support can influence the durability of regulation, infrastructure spending and corporate transition strategies.
Sport brings climate to new audiences
At the Nest Campus, athletes and health experts examined how rising temperatures, air pollution and extreme weather are changing sport.
Former professional athletes joined Alan Dangour, Director of Climate and Health at Wellcome Trust, to discuss adaptation and communication. Their involvement highlighted the ability of voices outside traditional climate institutions to reach audiences that policymakers and businesses may not.
Across Day 5, that same challenge appeared repeatedly.
The technologies needed for lower-carbon cities, buildings and power systems increasingly exist. The harder work lies in financing them, regulating their deployment, coordinating across jurisdictions and building public support.
For C-suite leaders and investors, Climate Week’s message is moving closer to execution. Climate strategy is no longer confined to targets and disclosures. It is becoming a question of capital allocation, asset performance, policy exposure and the ability to communicate why the transition matters to people now.

articles.full_text:
ADM Plans 800,000-Ton Carbon Removal Credit Offering from Nebraska CCS
- ADM plans to enter the voluntary carbon removal market with more than 800,000 tons of annual removal capacity from its Columbus, Nebraska, facility.
- Puro.earth is certifying the credits under its Geologically Stored Carbon methodology, with initial issuance expected by year-end pending audit completion.
- A 15-year crediting period could create one of the largest engineered carbon removal offerings to date, targeting buyers across technology, finance, aviation and pharmaceuticals.
ADM is preparing to enter the voluntary carbon dioxide removal market at significant scale. The agricultural commodities group plans to generate credits from its carbon capture operations in Columbus, Nebraska.
The facility has capacity to remove more than 800,000 tons of biogenic CO2 annually. ADM describes it as the world’s largest bioethanol carbon capture facility.
Puro.earth is currently overseeing certification and issuance under its Geologically Stored Carbon methodology, Edition 2024. Initial credits are expected by the end of 2026, subject to completion of the audit and verification process.
From Ethanol Production to Carbon Removal Credits
The project connects agricultural processing with permanent geological carbon storage.
ADM captures biogenic CO2 produced during ethanol fermentation at its Columbus corn processing complex. The company then purifies and compresses the CO2 before it enters Tallgrass’ transportation network.
Tallgrass transports the captured carbon to its Eastern Wyoming Sequestration Hub. There, operators inject it underground for permanent storage through carbon capture and storage wells.
The project operates under a Wyoming Department of Environmental Quality Class VI permit. ADM and Tallgrass inaugurated carbon capture and storage operations at Columbus in 2025.
“ADM has more than a decade of experience supporting carbon capture and geologic storage, including operating Class VI wells at our Decatur, Illinois, facility. That experience, together with Tallgrass’ CO2 transportation and sequestration system and the capabilities of other project participants, positions us to connect agricultural production with growing carbon removal markets at scale,” said Kris Lutt, ADM’s vice president of Innovation & Growth. “We’re already working with customers in our own value chains to help them meet their ambitious goals. This substantial carbon removal offering will allow us to expand our efforts to new customers across multiple industries, from technology and finance to aviation and pharmaceuticals.”
15-Year Carbon Credit Pipeline
If certification is completed successfully, ADM will begin a 15-year crediting period. That could create a substantial long-term supply of engineered carbon removal credits for corporate buyers.
The scale is notable for a market still working to expand the supply of durable removals. Buyers increasingly require robust measurement, verification and evidence of long-term storage when assessing carbon removal procurement.
RELATED ARTICLE: Whirlpool Builds Diversified Carbon Removal Portfolio
Jan-Willem Bode, President, Puro.earth, commented, “We are delighted to be working with ADM on this very exciting project. Certifying carbon removal at this scale demands real rigor, and we believe ADM has approached every stage – from measurement and data collection through to third-party audit – with the discipline and transparency that an investment-grade market requires. The audit process has run exceptionally smoothly, which is testament to the team ADM has built around this asset, and the hard work of the Puro.earth team coordinating with them. That partnership is what turns one of the world’s largest bioethanol carbon capture facilities into verified, investable carbon removal, and it sets a replicable benchmark for this sector worldwide.”
Agriculture Expands Its Role in Carbon Markets
The Columbus project also broadens ADM’s lower-carbon strategy beyond its existing agricultural supply chains.
The company employs more than 650 people in Nebraska. Its Columbus complex includes wet and dry mills that process corn into food ingredients, fuels and animal feed products.
ADM is also investing in regenerative agriculture, renewable natural gas and carbon capture. The company sees those businesses as opportunities to connect agricultural infrastructure with growing demand for lower-carbon products and carbon management.
“Our growth strategy is predicated on smart investments that build on our world-class footprint, and carbon capture is a great example of that. More broadly, we view agriculture as a powerful engine to lower carbon, and our capabilities uniquely position us to help deliver for stakeholders across value chains,” Lutt added. “From our leadership in regenerative agriculture, to our expanding capabilities in renewable natural gas, to our innovative work in CCS, we’re working to advance new ways in which agriculture can drive business results and power emerging lower-carbon solutions.”
For corporate buyers and investors, the project will test whether large existing industrial assets can deliver durable carbon removals at commercial scale. Successful certification would also add significant supply to a voluntary market where credibility increasingly depends on rigorous accounting, independent verification and permanent storage.

articles.full_text:
ERM, osapiens Partner to Turn ESG Compliance Data Into Business Action
- ERM and osapiens have formed a partnership combining sustainability advisory expertise with an AI-powered ESG data platform.
- The collaboration will support compliance across CSRD, CBAM, CSDDD and EUDR requirements, including supply chain due diligence and deforestation assessments.
- The companies aim to move ESG data beyond reporting, helping businesses use regulatory information for operational decisions, risk management and value creation.
Sustainability consultancy ERM has partnered with digital ESG platform provider osapiens to help companies manage increasingly complex sustainability data and regulatory requirements.
The partnership combines ERM’s advisory, technical and regulatory capabilities with osapiens’ AI-powered cloud platform. The companies will support businesses in collecting, validating and interpreting ESG data across their operations and value chains.
Their work will cover requirements linked to several major European Union regulations. These include the Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD), Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism (CBAM), Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD) and EU Deforestation Regulation (EUDR).
Beyond compliance, the partnership is designed to help businesses turn the information collected for reporting into data that can guide operational and strategic decisions.
Building ESG data infrastructure for compliance
ESG reporting requirements increasingly depend on large volumes of information that may sit across suppliers, business units and multiple jurisdictions. That creates challenges around data collection, quality, traceability and verification.
osapiens provides software-as-a-service tools designed to automate and secure ESG data collection. ERM’s specialists will review and validate the quality of information used and generated through those processes. They will also advise companies on the assessments feeding into ESG disclosures.
“As the sustainability reporting landscape continues to grow more complex, our clients are seeking solutions that will streamline their data collection to ensure regulatory compliance,” said Olaf Schatteman, Global Lead for Sustainable Product & Supply Chain Services at ERM.
“At the same time, they recognize that the data collected can be analyzed to generate meaningful insights about their business. Drawing on osapiens’ advanced digital and ESG data capabilities, we look forward to helping more organization harness data for business decision-making and value creation.”
RELATED ARTICLE: osapiens Acquires Nasdaq Metrio to Accelerate U.S. Expansion
From supplier screening to deforestation assessments
The partnership will also address ESG risks deeper within corporate value chains.
One application involves AI-enabled screening of multiple suppliers to identify ESG risks and support due diligence. Another combines satellite information with other data inputs for complex deforestation assessments under the EUDR.
These capabilities are particularly relevant as sustainability regulation moves further into supply chains. Companies increasingly need evidence about suppliers, sourcing locations and products rather than relying only on corporate-level disclosures.
“The businesses we work with are continually seeking to enhance their ESG data capabilities, and osapiens is therefore a welcome addition to ERM’s ecosystem of partners,” said Kushal Mashru, Head of Strategic Partnerships at ERM.
“By combining our digital, data and sustainability expertise we will help more organizations to navigate the ESG reporting landscape, with the ultimate aim of translating the data collected into the action required to operationalize sustainability throughout their operations.”
Compliance data becomes a strategic asset
For executives and investors, the partnership reflects a broader shift in ESG infrastructure. Regulatory reporting is creating datasets that can also inform procurement, supply chain oversight, risk management and capital allocation.
The value of those datasets depends heavily on their quality. Automated collection can improve efficiency, but businesses still need controls around methodology, validation and regulatory interpretation. The ERM-osapiens model combines technology with specialist review to address both sides of that challenge.
“Our partnership with ERM marks a significant step forward in helping organizations not only meet their ESG obligations but also use data to drive actionable insights and make an impact. Together, we’re enabling organizations to turn compliance into a catalyst for sustainable growth,” said Jaime Marijuán Castro, Head of Global Partnerships and Alliances at osapiens.
As sustainability rules expand across jurisdictions and value chains, ESG data systems are becoming part of core corporate infrastructure. For multinational companies, the challenge is no longer simply producing disclosures. It is building reliable information systems that can satisfy regulators while giving management a clearer view of environmental and supply chain risks.

articles.summary:
China’s expanding clean technology export machine is having a measurable impact on emissions far beyond its borders. New analysis estimates that Chinese exports avoided 374 million metric tons of carbon […]

articles.full_text:
China Clean Tech Exports Avoid 374 Million Tons of CO2
- 374 million tons: Chinese clean technology exports avoided an estimated 374 MtCO2 in 2025, exceeding the UK’s annual emissions.
- 6.9 billion tons: Over their lifetimes, China’s 2025 clean tech exports are expected to avoid 6,900 MtCO2, up 31% from 2024.
- $194 billion: China exported $194 billion of solar panels, batteries, wind turbines and electric vehicles last year, with emerging markets driving adoption.
China’s expanding clean technology export machine is having a measurable impact on emissions far beyond its borders. New analysis estimates that Chinese exports avoided 374 million metric tons of carbon dioxide in 2025.
That is more CO2 than the UK emitted over the same period.
The analysis comes from Lauri Myllyvirta, co-founder of the Helsinki-based Centre for Research on Energy and Clean Air. It covers exports of solar panels, batteries, wind turbines and electric vehicles.
The longer-term climate impact is considerably larger. Over their operating lifetimes, clean technologies exported from China in 2025 are expected to avoid 6,900 MtCO2. That is 31% higher than the equivalent estimate for 2024 and roughly twice India’s annual emissions.
China’s manufacturing scale reshapes clean energy economics
China occupies a complex position in the global energy transition. It remains the world’s largest carbon emitter while also producing much of the technology used to cut emissions elsewhere.
Its vast manufacturing base has pushed down the cost of solar panels, batteries, electric vehicles and wind turbines. That has changed the economics of electrification, particularly in emerging and developing economies.
“Current growth of solar and EVs, particularly in emerging countries, was not on anyone’s radar five years ago before China’s cleantech manufacturing boom,” said Myllyvirta.
“Just as the manufacturing boom led to increased supply and falling prices, the world experienced two fossil fuel price shocks in the past five years, giving adoption a further push. “
The combination of cheaper technology and volatile fossil fuel prices has strengthened the economic case for clean energy. It has also widened access to technologies that were previously more difficult for lower-income markets to deploy at scale.
RELATED ARTICLE: China Allocates $319M for Farm Disaster Prevention
South Asia emerges as a major beneficiary
Solar is responsible for a significant share of the emissions impact.
Almost one-third of the avoided emissions identified in the analysis came from Chinese solar exports to South Asia. Pakistan has emerged as a particularly striking example.
The country is experiencing a rapid solar expansion that has pushed its share of solar electricity generation among the highest globally. Low-cost Chinese panels have helped households and businesses adopt distributed solar as they respond to energy costs and grid constraints.
The trend shows how China’s manufacturing policies increasingly influence emissions trajectories outside its own borders.
For governments, the shift also creates a policy balancing act. Access to inexpensive Chinese technology can accelerate national climate and energy targets. At the same time, growing dependence on one manufacturing hub raises questions about supply-chain concentration, trade policy and domestic industrial competitiveness.
Clean tech exports become a $194 billion industry
The climate impact sits alongside a substantial commercial opportunity.
Chinese exports of solar panels, wind turbines, batteries and electric vehicles were worth $194 billion last year, according to Chinese customs data. Shipments had already reached $128 billion by June this year.
Those flows increasingly connect China’s industrial strategy with the investment plans of governments, utilities and companies across emerging markets.
For investors and corporate leaders, falling technology costs can improve the economics of renewable power procurement, electrification and clean infrastructure. Yet geopolitical tensions and trade restrictions remain important risks when assessing long-term supply chains.
Global emissions remain the larger test
The avoided emissions are substantial, but they remain modest against the scale of the global climate challenge.
Global carbon emissions reached about 39 billion tons in 2024, according to data compiled by Our World in Data. China’s exported technologies therefore address only a fraction of annual worldwide emissions.
Their importance lies in the direction and scale of deployment. China is no longer influencing the energy transition only through its domestic emissions or climate policies. Its manufacturing capacity is increasingly shaping how quickly other economies can access and deploy low-carbon technology.
As governments pursue renewable energy and electrification targets, the global impact of China’s clean tech sector will increasingly depend on where its products go, how quickly they are deployed and whether lower costs continue to accelerate adoption across emerging markets.

articles.full_text:
Explainer: Navigating the 45Z Clean Fuel Production Credit
The implementation of the Section 45Z Clean Fuel Production Credit represents a fundamental shift in how the federal government incentivizes decarbonization. Moving away from rigid technology mandates, this performance-based tax incentive rewards domestic fuel producers purely on their empirical climate impact. For ESG executives and energy investors, 45Z provides a transparent fiscal mechanism that turns carbon reductions directly into balance-sheet revenue.
However, unlocking this value requires navigating a strict operational landscape. Securing the maximum credit depends on precision asset tracking, rigorous supply-chain accounting, and mandatory compliance with federal labor standards. This guide breaks down the precise mechanical steps, data validation models, and regulatory guardrails companies must master to successfully claim the 45Z incentive.
“45Z sits alongside RINs and LCFS credits as one of several mechanisms that convert a fuel’s climate performance into realizable value for producers. For buyers, production-based credits are a relatively straightforward category to underwrite: the credit accrues as fuel is produced and sold, so volumes track physical output rather than project milestones.” – Fabian Roobeek, Head of Business Development US and Managing Partner, STX Group.
The Step-by-Step Mechanical Guide to Claiming 45Z
Under guidelines optimized by recent legislative updates, the 45Z credit covers qualified clean transportation fuels produced and sold through December 31, 2029. To legally qualify for and successfully secure the incentive, corporate taxpayers must execute a precise four-stage operational sequence:
RELATED ARTICLE: Homeowners Pile Into Solar Before Federal Tax Incentive Ends
- Mandatory Pre-Registration: Taxpayers must be registered with the IRS before the fuel is produced. Registration is filed via IRS Form 637 using specific activity letters: Code CA for Sustainable Aviation Fuel (SAF) producers, or Code CN for non-SAF transportation fuel facilities.
- Qualified Operational Sale: The clean fuel must be produced in the United States and subsequently sold to an unrelated person for operational transportation use.
- Lifecycle Emissions Modeling: Producers must calculate the fuel’s specific Carbon Intensity (CI) score at the facility level. Calculations must utilize the updated June 2026 45ZCF-GREET model released by the Department of Energy, which synchronizes backend calculations with current statutory changes.
- Annual Filing Execution: The tax credit is officially claimed at the end of the fiscal year by submitting IRS Form 7218 (Clean Fuel Production Credit) alongside the company’s corporate income tax return. A separate Form 7218 must be submitted for each individual qualified production facility.
Critical ESG Blind Spots & Risk Mitigation
- The Regional Feedstock Mandate: The IRS strictly enforces a North American sourcing rule (IRS Newsroom). To qualify for 45Z, 100% of the raw feedstocks must be grown or produced within the United States, Canada, or Mexico. This rule effectively disqualifies facilities relying on heavily imported foreign used cooking oils (UCO) or imported animal fats.
- The Labor Multiplier Effect: The baseline credit is a modest 20 cents per gallon (or 35 cents for SAF). To multiply this value by 5x to reach the maximum $1.00 per gallon (or $1.75 for SAF), facilities must satisfy federal Prevailing Wage and Apprenticeship (PWA) requirements. Any failure to meet these labor standards during facility construction or subsequent alterations triggers an immediate 80% reduction in the credit value.
- The GREET Data Bifurcation: The updated June 2026 GREET model introduces a complex compliance hurdle: companies with fiscal years spanning across the 2025–2026 transition must run the model separately for fuel produced before and after the shift, creating a bifurcated data and compliance requirement.
- Strict Anti-Stacking Violations: Tax law bars corporate double-dipping. A production facility cannot claim the 45Z credit for any tax year in which the project also claims carbon capture incentives under Section 45Q or clean hydrogen incentives under Section 45V.
Looking Ahead
With the U.S. Department of the Treasury moving 45Z to the final-rule stage in its unified regulatory agenda—targeting final action in November 2026—the policy environment has transitioned from open-ended uncertainty to a clear commercial planning timeline. Corporate sustainability officers must treat 45Z not merely as a tax strategy, but as a core operations and supply-chain mandate.

articles.summary:
