articles.full_text:
EU Weighs Delay to Methane Import Rules as Energy Security Risks Rise
- The European Commission is considering delaying methane reporting rules for imported oil and gas from January 2027 to January 2028 as governments raise energy security concerns.
- Companies that fail to comply with the EU law could face fines of up to 20% of annual turnover, while methane intensity limits are scheduled to apply from 2030.
- Industry-backed research says nearly half of EU gas imports could struggle to comply, while separate analysis argues sufficient compliant supply is available.
The European Union is weighing a delay to its landmark methane rules for imported oil and gas as tighter energy markets intensify pressure on Brussels to balance climate regulation with security of supply.
The European Commission is considering postponing the rules after France, the United States and more than a dozen EU member states raised concerns about implementation. The requirements are currently due to take effect in January 2027.
A one-year delay would push the start date to January 2028. Any change would require approval from EU governments and the European Parliament.
Europe’s methane rules reach beyond its borders
The EU legislation is the world’s first law designed to target methane emissions associated with imported fossil fuels.
From January 2027, foreign oil and gas producers supplying the bloc are due to face monitoring and reporting requirements for methane emissions. Companies that fail to comply could face fines equivalent to as much as 20% of annual turnover.
The regulation is set to tighten further from 2030, when the EU plans to impose methane intensity limits on imported oil and gas.
That gives the legislation considerable international reach. Europe is a major importer of fossil fuels, meaning its regulatory standards can influence production practices far beyond EU borders.
Methane is the second-largest contributor to climate change after carbon dioxide. It traps more heat than CO2 over shorter periods but also breaks down faster in the atmosphere. Rapid reductions can therefore have a relatively immediate effect on the rate of warming.
For oil and gas producers, emissions commonly come from wells, pipelines and other infrastructure. Canada, Norway and Nigeria are among countries that already regulate methane leaks from domestic fossil fuel production.
Energy security reshapes the political calculation
Pressure to delay implementation has increased as conflict in the Middle East disrupts global oil and gas markets.
French President Emmanuel Macron has requested a one-year postponement, arguing that the current timetable could create legal risks for importers as energy supplies tighten.
More than a dozen EU countries also called in June for the rules to be delayed or suspended. They include Germany, Europe’s largest gas market. Italy and the Czech Republic have pushed for a three-year delay.
Brussels attempted to ease concerns in July by advising countries to waive fines for companies breaching the requirements. Political resistance continued.
RELATED ARTICLE: EU Backs Greenland Strategy With $232 Million
The United States, now Europe’s largest supplier of liquefied natural gas, has also warned that the rules could disrupt EU fuel supplies.
The central concern is commercial. Producers or traders unable to meet reporting and verification requirements could decide against sending LNG cargoes to Europe if doing so exposes them to fines or legal uncertainty.
Those risks have become more politically sensitive as European gas inventories remain below normal seasonal levels amid elevated prices and disruption to Middle Eastern energy flows.
Italian utility Edison has said it expects no LNG cargoes from QatarEnergy until December 2026 because of the Iran conflict.
Industry and environmental studies reach different conclusions
A postponement to January 2028 would give importers additional time to establish compliance systems and secure independent verification of emissions data.
It could also allow companies to sign gas supply agreements covering the coming winter and subsequent periods without the immediate risk of violating the methane regulation.
The scale of the potential disruption remains contested.
A Wood Mackenzie study backed by the oil and gas industry and published in March found that nearly half of EU gas imports could face difficulties complying with the rules.
Research released by Rystad Energy for the Environmental Defense Fund in June reached a different conclusion. It found that ample gas volumes could meet the EU’s methane monitoring requirements, although companies would still need their compliance verified.
EU officials have also said assessing the regulation’s impact on supply contracts is difficult because many commercial agreements are not publicly available.
Brussels faces a climate and energy trade-off
The debate puts two EU priorities into direct tension: cutting methane emissions across fossil fuel supply chains and maintaining access to reliable energy during a period of geopolitical disruption.
For producers and importers, the immediate issue is regulatory certainty. A delay could provide more time to establish measurement, reporting and verification systems, but it would also postpone one of Europe’s most consequential attempts to extend climate standards across global fossil fuel markets.
The Commission has not confirmed when it will formally propose changes. Officials have indicated that a proposal could arrive soon.
Any revision will then move to negotiations between EU governments and the European Parliament. The outcome will determine not only when the methane requirements begin, but how far Europe is prepared to adjust climate regulation when energy security comes under pressure.

CSRWorks Expands EcoVadis Advisory Support Across Global Markets
- CSRWorks International has supported more than 500 EcoVadis assessments across North America, Europe, Asia Pacific and the Middle East.
- Around 60% of its clients have achieved Platinum or Gold medals, according to the company.
- Its EcoVadis advisory model spans gap analysis, sustainability management systems, questionnaire support, submission reviews and multilingual training.
Companies facing growing sustainability expectations across global supply chains are putting greater focus on the systems and evidence behind their ESG performance.
CSRWorks International is positioning its EcoVadis consulting and training services around that challenge. The company has spent more than a decade helping businesses prepare for EcoVadis assessments, address performance gaps and strengthen sustainability management systems.
As one of the longest-standing EcoVadis Strategic Partners, CSRWorks says it has supported more than 500 assessments worldwide. Its client base extends across North America, Europe, Asia Pacific and the Middle East.
Around 60% of those clients have achieved Platinum or Gold medals, according to CSRWorks.
From Assessment Gaps to Sustainability Systems
The advisory offering covers the full EcoVadis assessment cycle rather than focusing solely on questionnaire completion.
Companies can begin with a gap analysis of an existing EcoVadis scorecard or questionnaire. CSRWorks reviews the assessment to identify weaknesses, priority areas and potential missed scoring opportunities. It then develops an action plan for improving performance.
For companies requiring deeper support, consultants can help develop sustainability management systems aligned with EcoVadis requirements. That work can include policies, procedures, supporting documentation and tools for tracking key performance indicators.
Document readiness is another focus. Evidence submitted during an assessment must be relevant and aligned with the applicable criteria. CSRWorks reviews documentation before submission and helps companies develop structured processes for gathering sustainability data across internal teams.
The aim is to address immediate assessment gaps while building systems that can support future reporting and performance improvement.
Support Through the EcoVadis Questionnaire
CSRWorks also works directly with teams completing the EcoVadis questionnaire.
Its advisers provide guidance on performance information, supporting evidence and response strategy. For businesses that have already prepared their submission internally, a separate response-check service provides an expert review before submission.
The review identifies weaknesses, inconsistencies and opportunities to strengthen responses. Companies then receive recommendations intended to improve the quality and completeness of their final submission.
Smaller businesses can access a dedicated turnkey package. This is designed for companies with limited internal sustainability resources and covers the process from initial gap identification through documentation, evidence preparation and submission guidance.
RELATED ARTICLE: EcoVadis Opens Supply Chain Network Globally
Building Internal EcoVadis Capability
Training forms a separate part of the model.
CSRWorks provides public courses as well as customised in-house workshops. Programmes are designed to help employees understand the EcoVadis methodology, questionnaire requirements and scorecards.
Training also covers how teams can identify performance gaps and translate assessment results into improvement plans.
The company supports clients in English, Chinese, Japanese, Korean, Thai, Bahasa Indonesia, Spanish, Malay and other languages. That multilingual capacity allows programmes to be adapted for organisations operating across different markets and business cultures.
Why EcoVadis Readiness Matters for Global Business
For multinational companies and their suppliers, sustainability assessments increasingly sit alongside broader expectations around ESG governance, disclosure and supply-chain performance.
That makes assessment readiness more than a questionnaire exercise. Companies need credible policies, measurable performance indicators, supporting evidence and internal processes capable of producing consistent sustainability information.
For executives, the practical issue is how those systems connect. Procurement requirements, customer expectations and sustainability commitments can all depend on information held across different business functions.
CSRWorks’ advisory approach focuses on bringing those elements together while helping companies prepare for EcoVadis assessment requirements. For businesses operating across global supply chains, stronger internal sustainability systems can also support compliance readiness, customer engagement and longer-term ESG performance.

articles.full_text:
Reverion Raises $175 Million to Scale Dispatchable Clean Power Technology
- German energy technology company Reverion has raised $175 million in Series B funding to expand production of its reversible solid-oxide power systems.
- The company plans to increase annual manufacturing capacity tenfold to 250 MW, targeting utilities, heavy industry and data centres.
- Reverion says its systems achieve 74.2% electrical efficiency in generation mode while offering hydrogen production, energy storage and potential carbon-negative operation.
German energy start-up Reverion has secured $175 million in Series B financing to scale a technology designed to provide renewable power when wind and solar cannot.
The Bavarian company manufactures reversible solid-oxide systems that can operate as both electrolysers and fuel cells. They can convert surplus electricity into hydrogen or other storable gases, then reverse the process to generate electricity when required.
Most of the new capital will fund a production facility that expands Reverion’s annual manufacturing capacity tenfold to 250 MW.
“Solar and wind wind are vital, but their intermittency leaves grids vulnerable and forces heavy industry to rely on fossil-fueled backup power,” the company states. “Reverion provides the missing link: the Holy Grail of energy — a truly dispatchable renewable energy source that combines the clean credentials of renewables with the round-the-clock reliability of a conventional generator.”
Building a flexible asset for power markets
Reverion’s technology is designed to address one of the central challenges facing electricity systems with growing shares of variable renewable generation: providing firm power without relying on conventional fossil-fuel backup.
The company says its equipment has achieved electrical efficiency of 74.2% in generation mode. That figure was measured during live customer operation using units from pre-series production.
“The same system runs in reverse: in electrolysis mode, it converts surplus electricity into storable gases, giving operators a flexible asset that responds to price signals in both the power and gas markets.”
When biomethane is used as fuel, the system can capture high-purity carbon dioxide. Reverion therefore describes the plants as potentially carbon-negative. They can also operate using hydrogen without producing CO2.
“Solar and wind give us clean energy, but only when the weather cooperates,” said Reverion CEO Stephan Herrmann. “What the world needs is clean power on tap. By closing this Series B, we are laying the foundation for industrial mass production.
“We are building the dispatchable, carbon-negative engine that allows grids and heavy industry to run 100% clean, 24 hours a day, 365 days a year.”
Reverion currently has seven commercial plants operating in the field. Output per unit has also been increased to 500 kW.
Chief operating officer Felix Fischer added: “We are seeing explosive international demand for our systems as utilities and industrial customers recognize that true energy security requires dispatchable clean power. With seven commercial plants operating in the field and output per unit upgraded to 500kW, this capital ensures we can rapidly clear our backlog and steer the company toward long-term profitability.”
RELATED ARTICLE: Reverion Secures $41 Million in Carbon Removal Deals Led by Google, H&M
Data centres emerge as next growth market
Reverion is positioning data centres as a major commercial opportunity. Rapid growth in computing infrastructure has intensified concerns over grid capacity, electricity demand and emissions.
The company argues that its systems can use existing local gas infrastructure to provide on-site power where grid connections are constrained.
“Energy-intensive data centers are facing severe grid connection delays and mounting public pushback over environmental impacts. Reverion provides an immediate, on-site energy solution. By running on local gas infrastructure, Reverion allows data center operators to circumvent grid bottlenecks and secure continuous, firm power, turning energy-hungry infrastructure into a carbon-neutral or even carbon-negative asset.” Robert Trezona, CEO of deeptech and climate fund Kembara, which led the funding round, sees data centres as central to Reverion’s growth prospects.
“The growth market lies in powering data centers, where Reverion’s negative carbon footprint counts as much as efficiency. Hyperscalers need massive, reliable power, but they cannot compromise on their climate commitments.”
Investors back industrial scale-up
The Series B round also included Allianz, KfW Capital and climate-focused investment platform Carbon Equity.
Reverion previously raised $62 million in Series A financing in September 2024. It later received about $22.1 million from the European Innovation Fund. The company uses solid-oxide cells supplied by South Korea’s Doosan Fuel Cell.
For utilities, industrial groups and data-centre operators, the investment reflects growing demand for technologies that can combine renewable integration with firm power. Reverion must now demonstrate that its efficiency and carbon claims can translate from early commercial deployments into industrial-scale manufacturing.
Its planned 250 MW production capacity will provide a larger test of whether reversible solid-oxide systems can become a commercially significant part of the infrastructure supporting increasingly renewable power grids.

articles.title: Schroders, CalPERS Map $1.3 Trillion Adaptation Market
articles.summary:
Schroders has launched a new investment framework designed to help investors identify commercial opportunities emerging from the growing climate adaptation market. Developed in collaboration with the California Public Employees’ Retirement […]

articles.full_text:
Schroders, CalPERS Map $1.3 Trillion Adaptation Market
- Climate adaptation demand could reach $0.5 trillion to $1.3 trillion annually by 2030, as governments and businesses invest in resilience against worsening physical climate risks.
- Schroders’ new framework evaluates 102 adaptation activities, ranging from resilient infrastructure and water systems to early-warning technologies.
- The median activity could avoid $3.10 in economic losses for every $1 spent, although Schroders cautions that economic benefits do not automatically translate into investor returns.
Schroders has launched a new investment framework designed to help investors identify commercial opportunities emerging from the growing climate adaptation market.
Developed in collaboration with the California Public Employees’ Retirement System (CalPERS), the Climate Adaptation Investment Framework assesses 102 activities across infrastructure, technology, products and services.
The global investment manager, which oversees $1.1 trillion in assets, said the framework aims to separate the economic value of adaptation from its potential to generate investable returns.
That distinction is becoming increasingly important as capital flows toward infrastructure and technologies that can withstand floods, extreme heat and other physical climate impacts.
Adaptation demand could reach $1.3 trillion
Governments, businesses and communities face rising pressure to protect assets and economic activity from climate-related disruption.
The investment requirements could be substantial. Boston Consulting Group estimates annual demand for climate adaptation and resilience solutions could reach between $0.5 trillion and $1.3 trillion by 2030.
Potential spending spans resilient buildings, water infrastructure, flood protection, early-warning systems and other technologies designed to reduce exposure to physical climate risks.
However, a large addressable market does not necessarily create equally large investment opportunities. Some adaptation measures generate broad economic or social benefits without producing cash flows that private investors can readily capture.
Schroders’ framework is intended to help investors make that distinction.
“Investors have traditionally viewed the physical impacts of climate change primarily as a risk to their portfolios, but there is another side to that equation,” said Marina Severinovsky, Head of Sustainability, North America at Schroders. “Climate adaptation is increasingly becoming an economic and investment consideration in its own right, as businesses, governments and communities respond to a changing physical environment. Our aim with this framework is to give investors a clearer lens through which to understand how those changes could shape investment outcomes over time.”
RELATED ARTICLE: Schroders Publishes First-Ever Impact Investment Report
Economic benefits extend beyond investor returns
Schroders drew on existing approaches to defining and classifying climate adaptation to identify 102 activities for investment analysis.
Its findings point to a strong economic case for many resilience measures.
Of the activities assessed, 95 were modeled to prevent economic losses equal to or greater than their costs. The median activity generated $3.10 in avoided losses for every $1 of modeled expenditure.
For governments and companies, that calculation strengthens the financial case for investing before climate damage occurs. For asset owners, however, the question is more complicated.
The economic benefits of flood defenses, resilient infrastructure or warning systems can accrue across communities and supply chains. Investors therefore need to determine whether those benefits can support durable revenues and attractive risk-adjusted returns.
A framework for institutional capital
The collaboration with CalPERS brings an asset-owner perspective to that challenge. The US pension fund has increasingly incorporated climate-related risks and opportunities into its investment approach.
“The need to build resilience is clear and growing. Not all adaptation solutions are investable on purely commercial grounds today; however, the framework Schroders has developed gives asset owners and investors a practical way to assess, compare, and prioritize investments. We hope it encourages productive conversations that strengthen portfolio and economic resilience,” said Nelson Da Conceicao, Sustainable Investments Director, CalPERS.
For institutional investors, adaptation is expanding the climate investment conversation beyond emissions reduction. Physical climate risks increasingly affect infrastructure, property, supply chains and operating costs, creating both portfolio exposure and demand for resilience solutions.
The challenge is identifying where that demand can support scalable commercial models. Schroders’ framework offers investors a way to compare those opportunities while recognizing the gap between economic value and financial returns.
As adaptation spending rises, that distinction could become increasingly important to capital allocation. Investors will need to assess not only which solutions reduce climate losses, but where policy, public finance and private business models can turn resilience needs into investable markets.

articles.full_text:
Meta Backs MacroCycle rPET Plant With Multiyear Procurement Deal
- Meta will purchase environmental attribute certificates tied to recycled PET production from MacroCycle’s first commercial U.S. plant.
- The facility is expected to produce 5,000 tons of recycled PET annually from mixed and contaminated plastic waste.
- The multiyear agreement gives MacroCycle long-term demand intended to support financing and construction of its first commercial-scale facility.
Meta has signed a multiyear procurement agreement with MacroCycle Technologies to support the expansion of lower-carbon recycled plastics manufacturing in the United States.
Under the agreement, Meta will purchase environmental attribute certificates, or EACs, linked to recycled polyethylene terephthalate produced at MacroCycle’s first commercial plant. The facility will be built in the Southeastern United States, although its exact location has not been disclosed.
For MacroCycle, the deal provides long-term demand as it moves its recycling technology from development toward commercial-scale production. For Meta, it extends a procurement strategy already applied to lower-carbon materials such as cement and steel into plastics.
Turning difficult plastic waste into new PET
MacroCycle converts textile and packaging waste into recycled PET, or rPET, using its proprietary SolvoGenesis technology.
The solvent-based process dissolves and purifies PET while preserving its polymer chains. MacroCycle says this allows it to process mixed, blended and contaminated waste that conventional mechanical recycling often cannot handle.
Its first commercial plant is expected to produce 5,000 tons of rPET annually. The resulting material is designed to replace virgin PET made from fossil-based feedstocks.
“Most recycling forces a tradeoff,” says MacroCycle co-founder and CEO Stwart Pena Feliz. “Mechanical processes are cheap but degrade the material with every cycle and struggle with complex waste streams. Chemical processes that break PET all the way down to its monomers are energy-hungry and expensive. SolvoGenesis sidesteps that tradeoff,” he continues. “We dissolve and purify PET while keeping the polymer chain intact, which is why we can take the mixed, blended and contaminated waste that other processes reject and still come out with virgin-quality material at a fraction of the energy. The feedstock that is difficult for others to use is the feedstock we are built for.”
Meta uses procurement to support early-stage capacity
The agreement centers on EACs rather than direct ownership of the physical rPET output.
Such certificates can allow corporate buyers to support lower-carbon production and account for associated environmental attributes. MacroCycle says this approach can also create demand that helps emerging manufacturers secure financing for commercial facilities.
The company said Meta’s multiyear commitment provides the long-term product demand needed to support construction financing.
RELATED ARTICLE: Meta, MN8 Energy Sign 80 MW Solar PPA To Power U.S. Data Centers
That model could prove important for technologies facing the difficult transition from demonstration projects to commercial manufacturing. Securing predictable demand can reduce some of the market risk associated with building first-of-a-kind facilities.
Meta is applying a strategy it has previously used in other emissions-intensive material markets.
“Reaching net-zero means advancing lower-carbon solutions across our supply chain and in the materials we use,” says Devon Lake, head of net zero strategy at Meta. “We have been working to address emissions across our supply chain on materials like cement and steel, and our early procurement of materials from these sectors helped pave the way for the maturing markets we see now. We hope this transaction with MacroCycle will have a similar outcome in the plastics market.”
U.S. recycling capacity faces an import challenge
MacroCycle is also positioning the project as part of a broader effort to strengthen domestic materials production.
According to the company, the U.S. imports more than 40% of its virgin PET and over 20% of its rPET. It also says domestic recycled PET capacity is shrinking, creating the potential for greater reliance on imports.
Its planned facility would instead process plastic waste generated in the U.S. and return it to the domestic market as higher-value recycled material.
For companies pursuing supply chain decarbonization, the transaction illustrates how procurement can move beyond conventional purchasing. Long-term commitments and environmental certificates can help create revenue certainty for emerging manufacturing technologies.
The broader test will be whether early facilities such as MacroCycle’s can demonstrate competitive economics and expand beyond first-of-a-kind plants. If they do, corporate demand for lower-carbon materials could play a larger role in building domestic circular manufacturing capacity while addressing supply chain emissions.

articles.full_text:
Crédit Agricole Launches Natural Capital Division With $227M Forest Fund
- Crédit Agricole has launched Crédit Agricole Capital Naturel to provide financing, investment and advisory solutions for natural capital projects across Europe.
- Forests are the division’s first focus, supported by the planned majority acquisition of ecosystem restoration specialist EcoTree.
- Amundi is launching the Arbora Nova fund for institutional investors, targeting approximately $227 million for forest restoration and reforestation projects in France and Europe.
Crédit Agricole has launched a dedicated natural capital division as the French banking group expands its climate strategy beyond emissions reduction into ecosystem restoration.
Crédit Agricole Capital Naturel will initially focus on forests, bringing together financing, investment, insurance and project development capabilities. The group plans to extend the platform into water and biodiversity from 2027.
The bank said the division will serve companies, institutional investors, natural asset owners and local authorities. Its remit spans strategic advice, restoration projects, sustainable forest management, low-carbon transition projects and dedicated investment products.
Forests Become First Investment Focus
Forests will provide the first test of Crédit Agricole’s natural capital model.
The bank has entered exclusive negotiations to acquire a majority stake in EcoTree, a developer and operator of nature-based solutions. EcoTree has worked on European ecosystem restoration since 2018, including projects linked to carbon sequestration, biodiversity, water filtration and sustainable timber production.
Crédit Agricole is pairing this operating capability with institutional capital through Amundi, its asset management business.
The new Amundi Arbora Nova fund aims to mobilise approximately $227 million over time. It will invest in forest restoration, regeneration and sustainable development projects across France and Europe.
The strategy covers afforestation of land that has been bare for at least ten years and reforestation of severely degraded areas. Projects are intended to improve forest resilience, biodiversity and carbon storage while supporting the regional forest and timber economy.
Local economic development is also built into the model, including the use of regional businesses for forestry work.
Natural Capital Moves Further Into Finance
The new division will coordinate expertise across Crédit Agricole’s banking, insurance and asset management businesses.
Its offering will include advisory services, financing, insurance, investment products, project structuring and natural asset enhancement. This gives the bank several routes to serve companies seeking to reduce environmental impacts or strengthen sustainable supply chains.
It also creates investment opportunities for institutions seeking exposure to natural capital as an emerging asset class.
“Natural capital is the foundation of economic activity and regional resilience. Through Crédit Agricole Capital Naturel, we are harnessing the collective strength of Crédit Agricole to preserve and enhance natural capital. This initiative, initially focused on forests, is fully in line with our goal to be a leader in transitions and to sustainably support our customers, regions and economic sectors in the face of environmental challenges.” Grégory Erphelin, Deputy General Manager of Crédit Agricole S.A., in charge of Transformation, Human Resources and Transitions division
RELATED ARTICLE: Crédit Agricole Sets 90/10 Green to Brown Financing Target as Part of 2028 Transition Strategy
Climate Risk Raises the Economic Stakes
The launch comes as ecosystem degradation is becoming a more material economic and financial risk.
Crédit Agricole said nearly 670,000 hectares of French forests are affected by decay. The carbon absorption capacity of the country’s forests has also fallen by 24 million tonnes annually over the past two decades.
Meanwhile, the cost of natural disasters could rise by around 40% by 2050, increasing demand for adaptation and nature-based solutions.
The group already has significant exposure to this market. Crédit Agricole Assurances is France’s leading forestry insurer, while Amundi and Indosuez Wealth Management offer investment solutions linked to reforestation. Crédit Agricole CIB also structures and places market financing related to biodiversity and natural capital.
European Expansion Planned From 2027
Timothée Jaulin has been appointed Head of the Natural Capital Division and will oversee its rollout and product development. He previously held senior responsible investment and institutional partnership roles at Amundi.
For executives and investors, the structure is notable because it combines natural assets with mainstream banking capabilities rather than treating biodiversity as a standalone sustainability programme.
From 2027, the bank plans to broaden the platform beyond forests to water and biodiversity. That expansion could widen the range of projects available to companies and institutional capital.
Crédit Agricole’s approach also reflects a broader financial challenge. Protecting ecosystems requires capital at a scale that public funding alone may struggle to provide. By linking restoration projects with investment products, insurance and corporate financing, the bank is positioning natural capital within the financial infrastructure supporting Europe’s climate adaptation and regional resilience agenda.

articles.title: Behind the Crown: How Rolex Turned Quiet Values Into Its Strongest Statement
articles.summary:
In a milestone year, a record-breaking museum gift, 50 years of the Rolex Awards and a new podcast season reveal a commitment that speaks through the people it supports When […]
The post Behind the Crown: How Rolex Turned Quiet Values Into Its Strongest Statement appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Behind the Crown: How Rolex Turned Quiet Values Into Its Strongest Statement
In a milestone year, a record-breaking museum gift, 50 years of the Rolex Awards and a new podcast season reveal a commitment that speaks through the people it supports
When the National Geographic Museum of Exploration opened in Washington, D.C. this summer, visitors walked through 100,000 square feet of exploration history: Jacques Cousteau’s diving saucer, the pressurized suit Sylvia Earle wore for her record untethered sea walk in 1979, and photographs from more than a century of expeditions. What they found almost none of was watches.
That’s notable, because the museum’s largest donor was a watchmaker. Rolex described itself simply as the Founding Donor and Grand Opening Partner. The scale of its support became public only when watch journalist Jason Heaton, previewing the museum for Hodinkee, reported that a donor plaque listed Rolex’s gift at $100 million. The National Geographic Society had called it by far the largest single gift in its 135-year history when it was announced in 2023, without naming the amount. According to Heaton, the only Rolex on display in the entire museum is the Deepsea Challenge from James Cameron’s submersible.
On September 22, during New York Climate Week, Rolex will premiere the sixth season of Planet Visionaries, its documentary-style podcast hosted by climber Alex Honnold. The launch caps a year of milestones for the watchmaker’s Perpetual Planet Initiative, though Rolex, true to form, has kept the focus on the work rather than itself. Together, those milestones point to a single idea: Rolex’s most enduring asset may be its integrity, built through characteristic modesty and decades of work behind the scenes.
A commitment older than the trend
Over the past decade, corporate sustainability has moved in waves. Pledges and purpose campaigns surged, then retreated as companies grew wary of greenwashing accusations and political backlash. GlobeScan found that only 36% of consumers saw sustainability messaging from brands in 2025, down from 49% in 2023, and trust in the messages that remain has fallen too.
Rolex’s commitment predates that cycle by nearly a century. In the 1930s, founder Hans Wilsdorf began sending watches with explorers to the most extreme places on Earth. In 1953, Rolex equipped the expedition that put Sir Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay on the summit of Everest, and National Geographic’s coverage of the climb began a partnership that has now lasted more than 70 years.
Over time, the purpose of that exploration changed, from discovery for its own sake to protecting what explorers had found. In 2019, Rolex formalized that shift with the Perpetual Planet Initiative, which today spans more than 30 partners.
Letting others do the talking
What sets Rolex apart isn’t only the scale of its giving. It’s how little the company says about it.
Rather than commenting on its environmental work, Rolex lends its platform to the people doing it: oceanographer and Rolex Testimonee Sylvia Earle, whose Mission Blue has designated more than 160 ocean Hope Spots; Coral Gardeners founder and Rolex Testimonee Titouan Bernicot; and partners from Rewilding Argentina and Chile to explorer Steve Boyes’ Great Spine of Africa expeditions. Through its long-standing relationship with The Explorers Club, the Rolex Explorers Club Grant sends early-career researchers into the field. And as a partner to the OceanX Summit, held aboard the research vessel OceanXplorer in Singapore from October 7 to 9, Rolex joins the scientists, innovators and storytellers shaping the future of the ocean.
Rolex has also helped build the platforms that carry these stories. In 2019, it partnered with CNN to launch Call to Earth, a global initiative covering environmental challenges and the people working on solutions.
Planet Visionaries carries that approach into podcasting. Over five seasons, Honnold has interviewed Earle, actor Mark Ruffalo, SeaLegacy co-founders Cristina Mittermeier and Paul Nicklen, and conservationist Kris Tompkins. Season 6, produced by Sony Music Entertainment, runs 20 weekly episodes built around visual storytelling, on Rolex’s YouTube channel and major podcast platforms.
“This season of Planet Visionaries is about the people already doing that work every day,” Honnold said in a statement announcing the season. “Each guest saw a challenge and moved toward it, and their stories show just how much one person can set in motion.”
Why it matters now
The new season arrives as traditional outlets pull back from climate coverage. In February, The Washington Post laid off 74% of its climate desk, and CBS News no longer has a dedicated climate reporter. New York Times climate coverage has fallen 66% from its October 2021 peak, and global coverage dropped 14% in 2025.
But audience interest hasn’t faded, and podcasts are increasingly where these stories live, from HEATED’s new video podcast, produced by a former CBS News climate producer, to Drilled’s move to Pushkin Industries and the new season of Ayana Elizabeth Johnson’s What If We Get It Right?.
Rolex invested in the format before the latest wave of newsroom cuts, and has kept expanding it since. Planet Visionaries launched in 2021 as a four-part series and has grown into a 20-episode season built around video, one that gives its partners the microphone. Listeners respond to that approach: 61% say a branded podcast makes them more favorable toward the brand behind it.
Fifty years of backing people
Nowhere is Rolex’s consistency clearer than in the Rolex Awards, which celebrate their 50th anniversary this year. Created in 1976 as a one-time celebration of the Oyster, the first waterproof wristwatch, the Awards drew so much interest that Rolex kept them going. They have since supported 165 Laureates across more than 67 countries, whose projects have planted more than 50 million trees and protected 137 endangered species.
Some have changed their fields. Ophthalmologist Andrew Bastawrous turned a smartphone into a portable eye clinic across sub-Saharan Africa, and Felix Brooks-church’s flour fortification technology now delivers vital micronutrients to five million people in Tanzania.
This year’s Laureates, all women, are Pardis Sabeti (United States), Rachel Ikemeh (Nigeria), Rosa Vásquez Espinoza (Peru), Binbin Li (China) and Farwiza Farhan (Indonesia). All five appear on Planet Visionaries this season, alongside Krithi K. Karanth, the 2026 Rolex National Geographic Explorer of the Year.
Modesty as brand value
That consistency shows up in how the public sees the company. In RepTrak’s annual Global RepTrak 100, which measures corporate reputation across areas including citizenship, conduct and leadership, Rolex ranked first in the world in 2022 and placed in the top six every year from 2020 to 2025. RepTrak’s 2026 report found that consumers are placing greater emphasis on corporate behavior over corporate messaging, a shift that favors companies whose reputations rest on what they do rather than what they say.
That’s the paradox of Rolex’s approach. As other brands go quiet to avoid scrutiny, Rolex gains credibility precisely because it never made its commitment a marketing campaign. Decades of consistent support are difficult for competitors to replicate, and difficult for skeptics to dismiss.
Even Rolex’s disclosures have arrived quietly. Its sustainability report stayed internal for years before going public. It shows emissions down nearly 40% between 2021 and 2023, and about 70% of Rolex’s gold now reclaimed from its own production waste. Its 2025 key achievements include a new Swiss site aiming for the highest BREEAM green-building rating.
Rolex’s structure makes the long view possible. Privately owned by the Hans Wilsdorf Foundation, Rolex is free from quarterly earnings pressure and able to make commitments measured in decades rather than campaign cycles.
The result is a form of brand equity that doesn’t show up in advertising. It lives in a museum gallery that features explorers instead of watches, in a podcast that gives its airtime to scientists, and in fifty years of Laureates whose work has outlasted the sustainability trends around them.
In an era of loud pledges and strategic silence, Rolex has found a third path: do the work, support the people doing it, and let their stories speak.
Planet Visionaries Season 6 premieres September 22 on the Rolex YouTube channel, Apple Podcasts and Spotify.

articles.title: Amazon Energy Projects Add $11 Billion to US GDP
articles.summary:
Amazon’s investments in solar, wind, nuclear and battery storage contributed nearly $11 billion to U.S. GDP from 2023 through 2025, according to a new Oxford Economics study. The projects supported […]
The post Amazon Energy Projects Add $11 Billion to US GDP appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Amazon Energy Projects Add $11 Billion to US GDP
- Amazon’s carbon-free energy projects contributed nearly $11 billion to U.S. GDP between 2023 and 2025, according to Oxford Economics.
- The projects supported nearly 22,000 jobs annually, spanning construction, supply chains, operations and local services.
- Oxford Economics expects the portfolio to contribute more than $61 billion to U.S. GDP through 2034 and support about 23,500 jobs annually.
Amazon’s investments in solar, wind, nuclear and battery storage contributed nearly $11 billion to U.S. GDP from 2023 through 2025, according to a new Oxford Economics study.
The projects supported nearly 22,000 jobs annually during the period. They also generated billions of dollars in estimated tax revenue for communities hosting energy infrastructure.
The findings put an economic value on Amazon’s expanding energy strategy as electricity demand rises across the U.S. The company says it covers the costs associated with powering its data centers, rather than passing those expenses to surrounding communities.
Energy investment expands alongside data centers
Amazon now has more than 700 carbon-free energy projects across 28 countries. Together, they represent more than 40 gigawatts of capacity. The company says that is enough electricity to power more than 12.1 million U.S. homes.
Its portfolio includes utility-scale solar and wind, nuclear energy and battery storage. The investments create demand for construction workers, electricians, welders, suppliers and logistics companies. Operating projects also require plant managers, maintenance workers and technical specialists.
“Investment in America’s energy infrastructure has benefits that extend well beyond the electricity it generates,” said Pete Collings, managing director of economic footprint and sustainability at Oxford Economics. “Amazon’s purchases of carbon-free power support jobs and economic activity across the country, stimulate tax revenues that can pay for public services, and contribute to a more secure and resilient energy system.”
The assets can operate for 25 to 60 years, depending on the technology. Oxford Economics estimates their cumulative U.S. GDP contribution will exceed $61 billion through 2034. The portfolio could support roughly 23,500 jobs annually over that period.
States capture investment and tax revenue
Texas has Amazon’s largest state-level carbon-free energy portfolio, with more than 10 GW across solar, wind and nuclear projects. Between 2023 and 2025, the projects contributed more than $1 billion to state GDP. They also supported over 1,300 jobs annually and enabled more than $143 million in tax revenue.
“Corporate commitments to carbon-free energy are strengthening Texas’s reputation as a great place to do business,” said Bryn Baker of the Texas Energy Buyers Alliance. “Amazon alone has 10 gigawatts of carbon emissions-free energy capacity in the state, spanning solar, wind, and nuclear. Large energy customers want to grow their operations in the Lone Star State, and they are ready and willing to invest in the low-cost, reliable, carbon-free energy resources that can support that growth.”
RELATED ARTICLE: Amazon Adds 50+ Mercedes Electric Trucks in Germany
In Mississippi, Amazon’s projects contributed $212 million to GDP and supported about 280 jobs annually. They also enabled more than $22 million in tax revenue.
The state hosts Delta Wind, Mississippi’s first utility-scale wind farm. Developed by AES, the 184.5 MW facility began operating in April 2024. Landowners can continue farming around the turbines, combining agricultural activity with energy production.
“These are powerful examples of how we’re not only providing the carbon-free energy that companies like Amazon need to grow, but helping states like Mississippi attract critical investment, create new sources of revenue for landowners and local communities, and support sustainable economic growth for decades to come,” said Amanda Smith, vice president of external affairs, U.S. renewables and power, at AES.
Virginia projects contributed more than $331 million to state GDP and enabled over $15 million in tax revenue. Indiana recorded a $160 million GDP contribution and more than $11 million in tax revenue.
Energy demand becomes a C-suite issue
The figures arrive as data center growth increases scrutiny of electricity demand, grid investment and who ultimately pays for new infrastructure.
For executives and investors, the Oxford Economics analysis adds an economic dimension to corporate clean-energy procurement. Large power users are increasingly linking expansion plans with new generation, storage and grid capacity.
Amazon is also working toward its Climate Pledge commitment to reach net-zero carbon emissions by 2040. Its energy portfolio therefore sits at the intersection of climate strategy, infrastructure investment and digital growth.
As electricity-intensive technologies expand, the economic effects of corporate energy procurement will receive greater attention. Amazon’s U.S. portfolio illustrates how those investments can extend beyond operational power needs into jobs, tax revenues and long-lived regional infrastructure.

articles.title: UK Commits $3.3 Billion to Build Commercial Fusion Energy Industry
articles.summary:
The UK government is investing more than $3.3 billion over five years to turn six decades of fusion research into an industrial sector capable of supporting commercial power generation. Speaking […]

articles.full_text:
UK Commits $3.3 Billion to Build Commercial Fusion Energy Industry
- The UK government is committing more than $3.3 billion over five years to fusion research, infrastructure and commercialisation.
- The STEP prototype plant in Nottinghamshire will anchor efforts to build domestic supply chains, manufacturing capacity and fusion-specific skills.
- Commercial fusion electricity has yet to be demonstrated anywhere, leaving major technical and investment risks as governments position for a future global market.
The UK government is investing more than $3.3 billion over five years to turn six decades of fusion research into an industrial sector capable of supporting commercial power generation.
Speaking at the UK Fusion Forum, organised by the Fusion Industry Association on September 15, government and nuclear industry leaders said Britain is moving beyond scientific experimentation. The next challenge is building the companies, supply chains, skills and financing structures needed to deploy fusion at scale.
“The challenge before us is no longer simply proving the science, it is building the industry,” said David Capper, Director of New Nuclear and Fusion Energy at the Department for Energy Security and Net Zero.
Public funding shifts toward commercialisation
The government’s funding will support research and technology programmes, specialist facilities and the STEP prototype fusion power plant.
STEP is being developed at West Burton in Nottinghamshire. Its remit extends well beyond demonstrating whether fusion technology can generate power.
The programme is intended to develop the engineering expertise, manufacturing capacity, regulatory knowledge and supply chains required for future commercial plants.
Capper said the UK enters this phase with more than 60 years of fusion research behind it. It also has national laboratories, private developers, engineering companies, specialist suppliers, universities and investors already active in the sector.
A proportionate regulatory framework is another part of the government’s strategy. Rather than treating fusion under the same regulatory structures developed for conventional nuclear fission, Britain has established a separate approach tailored to its risk profile.
STEP becomes an industrial strategy
Tim Bestwick, CEO of the UK Atomic Energy Authority, said STEP is designed to tackle technical challenges while building wider industrial capabilities. “The opportunity for the UK is translating research leadership into industrial leadership”.
That opportunity could stretch beyond electricity generation. Technologies developed for fusion include superconducting magnets, advanced materials, robotics, remote handling and digital engineering. Many have potential applications across other industrial markets.
The UK Atomic Energy Authority has more than six decades of fusion research experience at its Culham Campus near Oxford. It serves as Britain’s national fusion laboratory and sits at the centre of the country’s emerging commercial ecosystem.
Yet significant uncertainty remains.
“Commercial fusion electricity generation has not yet been demonstrated anywhere in the world,” Bestwick said.
Even after that scientific hurdle is cleared, fusion plants will need to prove they can produce electricity at commercially viable costs. Programmes including STEP and LIBRTI, which focuses on tritium production, are addressing some of the technical barriers. Bestwick cautioned that considerable technical risk remains.
RELATED ARTICLE: UK Pledges $438 Million for Climate Security Risks
Fission experience shapes fusion investment strategy
Iain McNicol, Chair of the Nuclear Industry Association, said Britain’s established nuclear sector offers lessons for fusion without providing a direct blueprint.
“The United Kingdom was right to establish a proportionate regulatory approach rather than simply applying structures developed from fission,” he said.
For investors, one of the biggest lessons concerns project structure. McNicol argued that commercially investable frameworks must be established before projects seek large-scale financing. Promising technology alone will not secure deployment.
Supply chains must also develop before construction accelerates.
Future fusion plants could require advanced materials, high-temperature superconducting magnets, precision manufacturing, fuel-cycle technologies and complex systems integration. The Nuclear Industry Association represents more than 300 companies, many of which already work on safety-critical infrastructure and complex nuclear programmes.
Skills emerge as a critical constraint
Workforce capacity could become equally important as capital and technology.
“Projects do not fail only because they lack finance and technology,” McNicol said. “They fail when there are not enough engineers, technicians, welders, project managers and, yes, regulators.”
The government expects its fusion programme to support more than 10,000 jobs.
For executives and investors, the UK’s strategy is therefore about more than whether fusion science succeeds. Public funding is being used to build industrial capacity before commercial deployment becomes possible.
If fusion ultimately proves technically and economically viable, countries with established regulation, specialist workers and mature supply chains could capture a larger share of the market. Britain’s $3.3 billion commitment is an attempt to ensure its long-standing research base can compete for that industrial opportunity.

articles.title: ISO, UNDP Launch First Global Standard to Embed SDGs in Business
articles.summary:

The post ISO, UNDP Launch First Global Standard to Embed SDGs in Business appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
ISO, UNDP Launch First Global Standard to Embed SDGs in Business
- ISO/UNDP 53001 is the world’s first International Standard providing a management system specifically for integrating the UN Sustainable Development Goals into organizational strategy and operations.
- The requirements-based framework gives businesses, governments and institutions a consistent approach to setting SDG priorities, establishing objectives and measuring performance.
- The standard is designed to remain relevant beyond the 2030 Agenda, creating a longer-term framework that can adapt to future global sustainability goals.
ISO and the United Nations Development Programme have launched the world’s first International Standard designed specifically to help organizations turn the Sustainable Development Goals into measurable action.
Unveiled on the first day of the ISO Annual Meeting, ISO/UNDP 53001 establishes a structured management system for integrating the SDGs into strategy, governance and day-to-day operations.
The launch comes as companies, governments and institutions face greater scrutiny over how sustainability commitments translate into measurable outcomes. The new standard aims to provide a common framework for moving from broad pledges to implementation, performance measurement and continual improvement.
From SDG commitments to measurable performance
ISO/UNDP 53001 gives organizations tools to identify sustainable development priorities and establish related objectives. It also provides guidance for integrating those objectives into existing processes and tracking performance over time.
Importantly, it is a requirements-based management system standard. That gives organizations a consistent basis for demonstrating whether their approach meets defined requirements.
For boards, executives and sustainability teams, this could strengthen the connection between high-level SDG commitments and internal governance. It also creates a clearer structure for accountability and performance assessment.
ISO Secretary-General Sergio Mujica said organizations increasingly need practical mechanisms to implement the goals.
“The SDGs have provided a shared global vision for a decade. Today, organizations are looking for concrete ways to translate that vision into action,” Mr Mujica said. “International Standards have long helped organizations address complex global challenges by providing a common language and a shared framework for action. We are delighted to launch ISO/UNDP 53001 today, extending this proven approach to the SDGs and helping organizations create positive impact for people and planet.”
ISO and UNDP combine global networks
UNDP selected ISO as its international standards development partner for the initiative. The partnership combines UNDP’s sustainable development expertise with ISO’s standardization system and network of national standards bodies.
That structure is intended to make the framework applicable across sectors, geographies and different organizational sizes.
Marcos Neto, UN Assistant Secretary-General and Director of UNDP’s Bureau for Policy and Programme Support, said wider organizational participation remains essential to delivering the SDGs.
“The SDGs provide a shared blueprint for a more inclusive and prosperous future. Achieving that requires organizations everywhere to turn ambition into action,” Mr Neto said. “We are proud to launch ISO/UNDP 53001 alongside ISO as a crucial tool to help organizations embed the SDGs into the way they operate, lead and govern. By making sustainability part of everyday decision-making, the standard can help accelerate progress towards the 2030 Agenda.”
RELATED ARTICLE: ISO Sets New Global Standard for Environmental Performance
A common framework across sectors and markets
Developing a standard that could work across different industries and jurisdictions required international consensus.
Jens Heiede, Chief Executive Officer of Danish Standards, said the process brought together expertise from multiple sectors and countries.
“Creating a standard that could be applied by organizations of every size, sector and geography required extensive collaboration between experts from around the world. Together, we developed a practical and internationally agreed set of requirements that organizations can apply with confidence,” Mr Heiede said.
For companies operating across several markets, a common framework could help create greater consistency in how SDG priorities are managed internally. It may also give investors and other stakeholders a clearer basis for assessing organizational processes around sustainable development.
The standard arrives as the 2030 deadline for the SDGs approaches and attention increasingly turns to implementation and accountability.
ISO and UNDP have also designed the framework to extend beyond the current goals. ISO/UNDP 53001 can support future global sustainability objectives that succeed the 2030 Agenda.
That longer horizon gives boards and executives a framework intended to outlast the current SDG cycle. It also places sustainable development more firmly within management systems, governance processes and everyday organizational decision-making.

Germany Sets 2045 Deadline to Phase Out Fossil Fuels
- Germany has explicitly committed to transitioning away from fossil fuels by 2045, moving beyond its previous climate-neutrality pledge.
- Renewables are targeted to reach at least 80% of electricity consumption by 2030, supported by additional wind capacity and continued solar expansion.
- The roadmap puts electrification, grid investment and industrial decarbonisation at the centre of Europe’s largest economy’s energy transition.
Germany has committed to transitioning away from fossil fuels by 2045, setting an explicit national deadline for ending reliance on coal, oil and gas.
The roadmap, presented by Federal Environment Minister Carsten Schneider at the United Nations in New York, moves Germany beyond its previous commitment to climate neutrality. It sets out how Europe’s largest economy intends to remove fossil fuels from power, transport, heating and industry.
Germany becomes the third country, after France and the Netherlands, to publish such a roadmap. The move follows the COP28 agreement in Dubai, where governments committed to accelerating the transition away from fossil fuels.
Renewables Take a Larger Role
Electricity is central to Germany’s strategy. Renewable energy currently supplies about 55% of gross electricity consumption. The government wants that share to reach at least 80% by 2030.
The plan includes an additional 12 GW of onshore wind capacity. Germany is also pursuing continued solar expansion, alongside investment in electricity grids needed to support higher renewable generation.
Coal is scheduled to leave the power system no later than 2038. Meanwhile, additional dispatchable gas-fired power stations are expected to become capable of switching to green hydrogen. The government aims for climate-neutral, fossil-free power generation by 2045.
Germany has also committed to cutting methane emissions by 30% by 2030 under the Global Methane Pledge.
Transport and Heating Remain Critical
Delivering the roadmap will depend heavily on sectors where decarbonisation has proved more difficult.
Transport and heating continue to lag behind the electricity sector in cutting emissions. Electrification is therefore becoming increasingly important to Germany’s climate strategy.
By August 2026, about one-third of newly registered passenger cars were fully electric. The government is supporting adoption through means-tested incentives while expanding charging infrastructure.
Heating is also shifting. Heat pumps and district heating are intended to replace oil and gas systems. More heat pumps than gas central heating systems were sold in Germany for the first time in 2025, according to the government.
Yet the transition has faced political resistance. Germany’s heating rules became a prominent political issue after legislation sought to restrict new fossil-fuel heating systems.
Former German climate envoy Jennifer Morgan said faster implementation would be essential.
“Accelerating the shift from coal, oil and gas to clean renewables will bolster energy independence and insulate consumers from price shocks at a critical moment,” she said. “However, a roadmap is only the starting line.”
RELATED ARTICLE: Germany’s Institute for Ecological Economic Research
Industry Faces a New Investment Cycle
For German industry, the roadmap centres on electrification and modernisation. Public funding will support decarbonisation investments, while the EU Emissions Trading System will continue putting a price on carbon-intensive production.
The EU Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism will provide another layer of policy support as European manufacturers compete with imports from jurisdictions with different carbon costs.
For executives and investors, implementation will matter more than the 2045 headline. Grid expansion, renewable deployment, electrification and hydrogen infrastructure will determine how quickly capital shifts away from fossil-dependent assets.
Andreas Sieber, head of global political strategy at 350.org, called the explicit phaseout commitment a “notable shift,” while criticising continued government support for gas.
“The economic ministry keeps sabotaging the transition away from fossil fuels,” he said. “This year has shown in the starkest terms that fossil-fuel dependence is a risk for everyone as it exposes households and businesses in Germany and around the world to price shocks, volatility and geopolitical insecurity.”
Germany Adds Weight to Global Phaseout Push
Germany’s roadmap arrives as fossil-fuel dependence, energy security and climate policy remain closely linked to geopolitical risk.
The government is also extending its approach internationally. Its energy transition partnership with South Africa focuses on coal phaseout, renewable deployment and electricity-grid expansion.
Germany’s commitment gives the global fossil-fuel transition another national implementation test. For governments, companies and investors, the central question is now whether policy, infrastructure and capital spending can move quickly enough to turn a 2045 deadline into an investable transition pathway.

articles.summary:
The European Securities and Markets Authority has set out its 2027 priorities as the EU moves from designing capital market reforms to implementing them. ESMA’s annual Work Programme places deeper […]
The post ESMA Sets 2027 Agenda to Simplify and Integrate EU Capital Markets appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
ESMA Sets 2027 Agenda to Simplify and Integrate EU Capital Markets
- ESMA will expand supervision across ESG ratings, European Green Bonds, benchmarks, crypto-assets and critical ICT providers in 2027.
- Regulatory simplification, T+1 settlement and the European Single Access Point will form key parts of the EU’s Savings and Investments Union agenda.
- AI-based supervision, tokenisation and stronger data infrastructure will become increasingly central to oversight of European financial markets.
The European Securities and Markets Authority has set out its 2027 priorities as the EU moves from designing capital market reforms to implementing them.
ESMA’s annual Work Programme places deeper market integration, regulatory simplification and expanded supervision at the centre of its agenda. The regulator will also increase its use of data, artificial intelligence and technology to oversee increasingly complex financial markets.
The programme sits within ESMA’s 2023–2028 strategy and supports the EU’s wider Savings and Investments Union, or SIU. The initiative seeks to channel European savings towards productive investment while building deeper and more competitive capital markets.
Verena Ross, Chair of ESMA, said: “2027 marks an important milestone for the Savings and Investments Union (SIU) as many of ESMA’s strategic initiatives move into the delivery phase. While co-legislators continue their work on the Market Integration and Supervision Package (MISP), ESMA is already advancing on key elements of the SIU agenda including initiatives to simplify the regulatory, reporting and supervisory framework. ESMA also continues to modernise the way it supervises markets through greater use of data and technology. This work programme reflects ESMA’s commitment to strengthening the Single Market, protecting investors and safeguarding financial stability. It enables ESMA to remain agile in the face of volatile and risky market conditions, while responding effectively to rapidly changing needs and priorities. As financial markets continue to evolve, I know that ESMA and its staff will remain focused on ensuring that EU capital markets are efficient, resilient and attractive.”
ESG ratings and green bonds enter expanded supervision
ESMA’s supervisory footprint will broaden substantially during 2027.
The regulator will advance oversight of consolidated tape providers and external reviewers of European Green Bonds. It will also process applications from ESG rating providers and begin supervising the sector.
That brings ESG data and assessments further into the EU’s regulated financial architecture. Investors and companies increasingly rely on these ratings for capital allocation, risk management and sustainability strategies.
ESMA will also adapt to expanded responsibilities for benchmark administrators.
Digital resilience is another priority. ESMA will work with other European Supervisory Authorities to oversee critical third-party ICT service providers. It will continue monitoring compliance with the Digital Operational Resilience Act, or DORA, across its supervisory responsibilities.
The regulator will also review the effects of EMIR 3 reforms on EU clearing markets. Policymakers want European clearing houses to remain resilient while reducing reliance on certain systemically important clearing services outside the bloc.
RELATED ARTICLE: ESMA LAUNCHES CALL FOR EVIDENCE ON ESG RATINGS
EU pushes ahead with capital market integration
Market integration will remain closely tied to the Savings and Investments Union.
ESMA expects EU co-legislators to reach a final agreement on the Market Integration and Supervision Package in 2027. The regulator will then prepare for changes to its mandates and responsibilities.
Other major projects are already moving forward. These include implementation of the European Single Access Point and Europe’s transition to T+1 securities settlement.
ESMA will also support implementation of the Retail Investment Strategy, with investor protection and accessible financial information remaining priorities.
Four simplification initiatives will advance during the year. They cover transaction reporting, funds reporting, the retail investor journey and risk-based supervision.
The goal is to reduce unnecessary administrative burdens while improving the quality and usability of regulatory data. ESMA also wants supervision to become more targeted and effective.
For financial institutions, the direction is significant. EU policymakers are seeking to simplify compliance without weakening market oversight or financial stability safeguards.
AI, tokenisation and data reshape supervision
Technology will become more embedded in ESMA’s own supervisory model.
The authority plans to expand its Data Platform and deploy AI-based tools to support supervision. Cybersecurity capabilities will also be strengthened as financial markets become more digitally interconnected.
ESMA will continue work on crypto-assets, including supervisory convergence with national authorities overseeing crypto-asset service providers under MiCA.
Artificial intelligence’s wider impact on financial markets will receive further attention. Tokenisation will remain another priority as ESMA examines its potential role in European capital markets.
For executives and investors, the 2027 programme points to a more integrated supervisory environment across sustainability, technology and traditional financial markets. The challenge for Europe will be balancing simpler regulation with stronger oversight as it seeks deeper pools of capital and greater global competitiveness.

articles.title: Germany, Austria and Luxembourg Launch $2.5 Billion e-SAF Scheme
articles.summary:
Germany, Austria and Luxembourg have opened a $2.5 billion funding mechanism aimed at accelerating Europe’s market for electricity-based sustainable aviation fuel. The programme is the first concrete project under the […]
The post Germany, Austria and Luxembourg Launch $2.5 Billion e-SAF Scheme appeared first on ESG News.
articles.full_text:
Germany, Austria and Luxembourg Launch $2.5 Billion e-SAF Scheme
- Germany, Austria and Luxembourg have launched a joint $2.5 billion funding mechanism to narrow the price gap between e-SAF producers and buyers.
- Around 50 synthetic aviation fuel projects across the EU are awaiting final investment decisions, according to the European Union Aviation Safety Agency.
- The double-auction model aims to give producers long-term revenue certainty while allowing airlines and fuel buyers to maintain shorter procurement cycles.
Germany, Austria and Luxembourg have opened a $2.5 billion funding mechanism aimed at accelerating Europe’s market for electricity-based sustainable aviation fuel.
The programme is the first concrete project under the eSAF Early Movers’ Coalition, established in December 2025. It targets one of the biggest obstacles facing Europe’s emerging e-SAF industry: the gap between the price producers need to finance projects and what aviation fuel buyers are prepared to pay.
The intervention comes as policymakers push to translate Europe’s aviation decarbonization mandates into new production capacity.
A test for Europe’s e-SAF pipeline
Europe has built a sizeable pipeline of proposed synthetic aviation fuel projects, but many have yet to secure financing.
The European Union Aviation Safety Agency, or EASA, says roughly 50 synthetic aviation fuel projects across the EU are awaiting final investment decisions.
For developers, securing long-term buyers remains critical. Production facilities require substantial upfront investment, while airlines and other fuel buyers have generally favored shorter contracts. They have also been reluctant to commit to higher future prices without greater certainty.
The three-country programme is designed to address that mismatch directly.
Germany will provide up to $2.4 billion, accounting for most of the funding. Austria and Luxembourg will each contribute up to $71 million.
Subsidized e-SAF volumes will be allocated among the countries according to their respective funding contributions. The programme remains subject to European Commission approval under EU state aid rules.
Double auctions tackle the price gap
The mechanism uses separate competitive auctions for e-SAF producers and buyers.
An intermediary will establish clearing prices through the two processes. Public funding will then cover the difference between the price required by producers and the amount buyers are willing to pay.
The structure is intended to provide developers with the revenue visibility needed to support investment decisions without requiring airlines to assume the entire cost premium.
Dagmar Fehler, chief executive of NOW GmbH, which is supporting Germany’s transport ministry on the programme, described the mechanism as the link between long-term investment security for producers and the shorter procurement cycles buyers typically use.
Austria’s mobility minister, Peter Hanke, said the joint funding was “sending a strong signal in favour of establishing a European market for renewable fuel,” adding that the scheme was “creating long-term prospects for producers, promoting transparent price signals and helping to ensure that e-SAF will also be available in Austria.”
RELATED ARTICLE: Argus Launches SAF Emissions Cost Indexes
EU mandates raise pressure on supply
The programme sits within the EU’s ReFuelEU Aviation framework, which is steadily increasing sustainable aviation fuel requirements.
SAF must account for 2% of aviation fuel supplied at EU airports in 2025. That requirement rises to 6% in 2030 and 70% by 2050.
EASA data show suppliers delivered 39.3 million tonnes of aviation fuel at EU airports in 2025. SAF accounted for 1.1 million tonnes, or 2.8%, putting supply above the initial mandatory threshold.
Yet those figures also expose Europe’s supply-chain challenge.
Used cooking oil accounted for 80% of SAF supplied, while 85% of feedstocks originated outside the EU. E-SAF, produced using renewable hydrogen and sustainable carbon, remains a marginal part of the market.
Investors watch whether mandates become bankable projects
For hydrogen developers and electrolyzer suppliers, the coalition offers a price-risk backstop in a sector where uncertain offtake has delayed investment decisions.
For governments, the programme will test whether coordinated national funding can accelerate production while the European Commission considers a broader EU financing mechanism.
The stakes extend beyond aviation. A functioning e-SAF market could create additional demand for renewable electricity, hydrogen and carbon-management infrastructure across Europe.
Success will ultimately depend on whether the auctions convert planned projects into operating capacity. If they do, the three-country model could offer Europe a practical route from aviation mandates to a more domestic, hydrogen-based fuel supply.
